speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
Railways and Canals-Welland Ship Canal- construction, $8,000,000.
Will the minister state how the $5,000,000 appropriation for this item stood at the end of the fiscal year?
That appropriation was all used up last year, and in addition there was expended $435,000 under a supplementary estimate.
With reference to the increase in the appropriation for this year, perhaps the minister would tell the committee what work is proposed to be done.

The details in connection with the proposed expenditure of $8,000,000 are as follows: Sections 1 and 2, $2,000,000; sections 3 and 4, $2,700,000; section 5, $800,000; gravel, $40,000; sand, $200,000; cement, $1,000,000; metal work for locks, $330,000; timber, lock 1, $35,000; bridge superstructure, $250,000; moving superstructure, Grand Trunk bridge No. 11, $25,000; land expropriated not paid for, $110,000; engineering staff, $410,000; construction railway staff, $100,000; making a total of $8,000,000.
Would the minister inform the committee how the work is being carried on, whether on straight contract or cost-plus basis?

Sections 1, 2 and 5 are being carried on under straight contract. On sections 3 and 4 the work was on a cost-plus basis. We have asked for tenders, and they are now in, and will be considered within the next day or two.

What new
contracts have been entered into this year in connection with this work?
No new contracts.

Can the minister give the committee some information about any new scale of rents that the department is charging for water-power in connection with our canals? I believe that the new plant near Peterborough is coming into operation. What does the Government propose to charge the HydroElectric for that service?
That matter is under consideration and has not been determined.

What does the Dominion Power Company, of Hamilton, pay for the power rights it has on the old Welland canal?
Supply-Welland Canal
I am afraid I cannot give that information offhand, but I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend at an early date.
Also the information on the other point.
I shall be delighted.

Will the minister tell us something of the present status of the work,-what new construction is ahead, how far this appropriation will go towards completing the work, and what the condition of the canal will be when the work is completed? I have been told that the channel both above and below the canal is such that when this work is completed the canal will be s'.e to accommodate no larger boats than are now using the old canal; in other words, that this new construction will add comparatively little to the navigability of that water route.

The original estimate of the cost of the whole canal was $50,000,000. Contracts for sections 1, 2, 3 and 5 were let in 1913, at an estimated value of $20,350,000. When the contracts were abandoned under agreement early in 1918, the total expenditure on the work to the end of 1918, including the purchase of plant, material and stores from contractors was $16,069,000. Work was resumed under cost-plus agreements in January, 1919, and total expenditure to March 31, 1921, was $25,340,000. Early in 1921, Section 5 was put under contract; later in the isame year, Sections 1 and 2 were combined and re-let; and at present Sections 3 and 4 are about to be placed under contract. The estimated value of a schedule-rate contract for completion of Sections 3 and 4 combined is $16,500,000, which includes $2,000,000 for plant and stores which the successful tenderer will have to take over. The estimated amount yet required to fully complete the canal from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario is $55,000,000.

Will the minister say what will be the position of the completed Welland canal in relation to the proposed further improved waterways system in order to allow the passage of seagoing vessels to the ports of the upper lakes?

When this
canal is completed, I understand, there will be a depth of 25 feet available for vessels,

as against 14 feet in the old canal. There will be that additional draught which will mean increased tonnage.

Could that
depth of 25 feet be extended to say 30 feet without entailing any very great additional expense, or without interfering with navigation?
Mr, KENNEDY (Essex) :	I understand that could be done without interfering with navigation, and that all the locks are being built with an extension to a depth of 30 feet in view.

Do I understand that
when this work is completed it will be possible for vessels of 25' feet draught to enter from either end of these canals? Will the lock depths and the depth of the route up through the Detroit river be sufficient to accommodate vessels of that draught?

As I understand, at low water on the Limekiln crossing on the Detroit river there is a depth of 21 feet. Of course this canal will not be finished for some years, and by that time there may be considerable difference in the depth Available for vessels passing up and down the lakes.
I understand the minister to say that the estimated cost of completing the canal is $55,000,000? What amount has been spent already?
Approximately $30,000,000. Fifty-five million dollars was the estimated cost when the work started.
And that is the estimated cost now for completing it?
Yes.
In what period of time, assuming that normal conditions prevail, do you expect to complete the work?

We expect
to have these five sections completed in 1927.

Would that be the
whole canal?

There are
nine sections jaltogether. The date of completion depends absolutely upon how much money there will be available and how readily we can obtain it.

Supply-Welland Canal

Unless the conditions
are favourable it will not be completed in 1927?

Does the
Government intend to avail itself of the cooperation of the United States?

Will there be any benefit to navigation from the expenditure already made until the canal is actually completed?
Mr. KENNEDY	(Essex) :	The	depth
for boats of the draught in use to-day is 14 feet, but they will have only seven locks instead of twenty-four as at present.

What I am asking the
minister is this:	Presuming we spend the
$55,000,000 in addition to moneys already spent, estimated to complete the work at present under construction will it benefit navigation?
Mr. KENNEDY	(Essex):	Yes.

In what	way?
Mr. KENNEDY	(Essex) :	The sum	of
$55,000,000, it is estimated, will complete the whole canal.
If the money was available in all probability it would.

In view of the present financial condition of the country could we not get along very well without doing any more work upon this canal? I may say that in the town of Windsor, in the county of Hants, the country owned certain wharves, but in 1914 the government leased them to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and to-day the small lumbermen are paying 75 cents a thousand for shipping lumber over those wharves. If the minister is going to spend some eight or nine millions of the people's money at the present time on canals, I think he should at least take those wharves back from the Canadian Pacific and give the people of the county of Hants their wharfage for nothing, and remove that handicap from the lumber industry.

I would like to ask the minister this question: When this canal is completed, if there is no further work to be done on the St. Lawrence farther down the river, would it be possible for vessels of 25 feet draught to get into lake Ontario?
When this canal is completed the largest vessel that is now on the lakes will be able to go as far as Port Colborne, and then on to Kingston and Prescott.
If we were to stop construction at the present tame, except in regard to existing contracts, how much of this estimated expenditure could be dispensed with until we have more money in our treasury?

That is rather a difficult question to answer. When we took up the question of the estimates for this year we went very thoroughly into the matter with a view of seeing whether it was possible to curtail the expenditure in view of the financial condition of the country. But in the case of at least three contracts we found that the material was on hand and that it would depreciate, and the expenditure of some $20,000,000 would be jeopardized. We therefore thought, after giving the matter every consideration, that the best thing to do would be to carry on as economically as we could in the meantime.
What proportion of the work on the canal has been completed?
My recollection of the figures formerly given, and I think they are correct, is that about 33 per cent is finished at the present time.
And the expenditure has been in the neighbourhood of $25,000,000 so far.
Thirty millions.
At that rate the total expenditure would be approximately $90,000,000, whereas the minister told us a few minutes ago that the total cost would only be $55,000,000.
Well, the cost of the plant is included in that $30,000,000.

I presume the cost
of the plant would be $4,000,000. Excluding that, the total amount would be in the neighbourhood of $75,000,000. And it miust be remembered that since the canal has been started contracts have been let time and again at an advanced price.

I wish to say I am thoroughly in accord with the plans of the Government in going on with the deepening of the Welland canal; I think it is
Supply-Welland Canal

in the interest of the transportation service of this country. It is absolutely in harmony with our projects for improving the transportation systems of Canada, and lowering freight charges. All I regret is that the Government has not pushed its proposals more vigorously. I know there are financial reasons, perhaps, for not proceeding, but the sooner that work is done the better for the country and the sooner the Government decides to accept the offer of the United States the better. The United States have, for the first time, made an offer to co-operate with Canada in the direction of deep waterways that will allow the passage of seagoing vessels to the upper ports of lake Superior, to the great benefit of western Canada especially, which will give us a real competition in the matter of transportation charges of wheat and things of that kind.
What about the railways?

My hon. friend is very sore about the railways. Let him go to the committee of this House considering freight rates at the present time, if he wants some information, and he will get some surprising information. But the point I wish to make-and I say it on behalf of the commercial interests of Canada, and the agricultural interests of the West, especially-that you do not often get a proposal made of this character by the neighbouring country, with the money it has at its disposal. It would probably be an easy thing to make a joint arrangement, as between Canada and the United States, for the early completion of the deep waterways from the St. Lawrence right up to the upper ports of lake Superior.

I would like to ask the
minister if the argument submitted in favour of continuing the work would not apply equally as strongly to some other projects? I have in mind the completion of the Hudson Bay railway.

We might
discuss that later in the afternoon.
Mr. STEWART (Lanark). With reference to the question of unemployment which has just been raised, I would like to make it perfectly clear that, so far as the continuation of this work is concerned, there is no question in this section of the House. But I desire to draw the attention of the House to the fact that in the contracts, as I understand them, that still

exist in connection with this work, there is a provision that the work could be discontinued. I would like to have the minister give us a statement as to that-that is that the continuation of the - rk is a matter within the discretion of the Government and of the House.
I understand that is correct. If the Government does not vote the amount, the contract will be suspended.
In view of the unemployment situation, perhaps never more severe than now, probably, the minister will consider it very unwise to take such a step.

I want to get a little
information from the minister as to what real value the Welland Canal will be in the haulage of grain until the deepening of the St. Lawrence is carried out, and the work has been advanced so that it will enable the grain to be carried in large lake freights eastward as far as Kingston and Prescott. I cannot see that that will be of any very great advantage as reducing the transportation cost of grain. As a matter of fact, there are boats of comparatively small draught now that run from Fort William to Montreal, and the carriage of grain in large vessels down to Kingston will not prevent them from using the smaller boats for the whole distance. I believe that essentially the Welland canal project is a sound one, but it should certainly never have been undertaken until the whole scheme could be carried out, and these 20 and 25-foot vessels provided to carry the grain right through from Fort William to Montreal. I was opposed to the grant a year ago, and I see no reason for changing my position now. I quite realize that it might be a very costly thing to leave work, upon which twenty five or thirty millions have been spent and not carry it through. In other words, when you get a job half done it may be more expensive to leave it in that condition than to complete it. I would like to have some information from the minister upon that point, I wish to say that the results that will come from the completion of the Welland canal in itself, as far as moving grain from Fort William eastward is concerned, will be very small indeed.

I may, perhaps, give the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) some information on this subject,

Supply-Welland Canal
as I have been connected with transportation matters more or less for a few years. With reference to the ships that come down from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne and Buffalo, I do not know just what their grain rate is, but I think it is li cents a bushel. It is true they often get a return cargo. They carry from 450,000 to 750,000 bushels of wheat. If the Welland canal were deepened today the boats would go to Prescott, and it is a cheap proposition from Prescott to Montreal,-probably half a cent a bushel would cover the cost of taking it to Montreal, and putting it on the ocean liner, or into the elevators. As a matter of fact, my information is:-and I believe it to be accurate, because it is obtained from the best sources of information-that it would take practically seven boats, to-day to bring what the Grant Morgan would carry from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne, going through the canal. I think the highest capacity of these boats is about 100,000 bushels, and the average would be about 80,000 bushels. These large boats could run to Prescott for another cent or two, as against five cents, which is the cost today. Of course, the rates would vary. When you get a straight rate, it varies from four to eight cents, depending on how anxious they are to get the cargoes. It takes seven or eight of these smaller boats to carry what one of the large boats can handle, and the large boats have only about two more of a crew, so that the cost of operation of one of these small boats is about the same as the cost of the operation of a large up-to-date freighter. By this means relief would be given to the extent of about 3 cents a bushel to the farmers of the West, and I believe the St. Lawrence project would probably give them relief to the extent of another cent and a half. I favour the speeding-up of the Welland canal. There is competition between the two routes from the head of the lakes, between the line that goes through Canada to Montreal, and the line that goes through the United States to New York. The Americans have the use of our canal for nothing, and if they want to pay half the cost, let them do it. You cannot put a dollar into our canals, but the United States gets five times the benefit that Canada receives. The United States is willing to pay, and I do not know any reasoi^ under the existing conditions why she should not pay her
share. There is no international complication that I can see, because you are going to have all the money necessary for our purposes. There is no reason why, if the United States are getting ten times the benefit of the canal, they should not pay their share. And the only reason they are making this offer to us is because it is worth ten times as much to the farniers of the United States as it is to our farmers. It would make a difference of 4 cents a bushel on the price of the wheat on the continent. That is a great deal of money. What influences are today at work to stop the St. Lawrence project, and prevent our friends in the Cabinet from conferring with the United States, I have not the slightest idea.
Personally, I think it is extraordinary that when the government of the great United States wants to talk about a project of this kind, one that affects vitally every farmer on the northern part of the American continent, we cannot at least listen to what they have to say. I am absolutely in accord with the statement that has often been made that the carrying out of this great project will mean a difference of three cents a bushel to the farmer, and I do not believe the railways of this country will suffer materially, because what has heretofore come by rail will continue to come that way. Some arrangement should be made about the matter in this way. The reason that we are getting via Montreal a great deal more grain than is going via Portland is because our transportation facilities are better than those of the United States, and as regards freight rates we are beating the Americans by two cents a bushel. Last year 47,000,000 bushels came to Montreal out of Chicago, and it comes a little earlier than the wheat of the Canadian Northwest. We should have some control of that situation, because it should not be possible for the situation to arise that when our Canadian wheat is being transported, the Canadian farmer finds that the elevators are already filled up with United States wheat that has come through our canals free. That is only an [DOT]incidental matter; but you have to consider it. Wheat ripens in the United States two or three weeks earlier than it does in Canada, so that they are ready to transport it sooner than we are. Last year 138,000,000 bushels were shipped out of Montreal, and 47,000,000 bushels of that came from Chicago, for the first time in the history of the country. This grain is going to come
Supply-Welland Canal

more quickly in future, and Montreal is found to be one of the greatest ports on this continent; nothing can stop that. There can never be any really intelligent opposition to this project from Montreal, and I do not think there is any. There is only one place as vitally situated as it is, although there may be certain ports that will store wheat at the head of the Great Lakes. The Canadian farmer is vitally interested in the price of wheat, and the price that he receives for his wheat depends upon the price of wheat at Liverpool and the cost to transport it to that city. If you can lessen the cost of inland transportation by three cents a bushel, you are going to make the price of wheat to the farmer three cents higher, because that will be the price for wheat grown west of the Great Lakes.

I recognize the force of the argument of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), and it may be that the completion of the canal with the considerably larger vessels that can pass through it, will bring about the result, or, at any rate, part of the result that he has stated. I will admit that that aspect of the question is one that I have not looked into very closely. I believe, however, that it would mean the erection of elevators at Prescott and Kingston for the transfer of this grain from the lake vessels that brought it down to those points, to the barges that would carry it on to Montreal. What expense would be involved in doing that, is also a matter for consideration. I am free to admit, though, that my hon. friend in that respect may have substantial reasons to support his argument. My whole attitude to the question was rather governed by the idea that we should control, as much as possible, our public expenditures, in view of our financial situation, and I still think that is a consideration that should weigh with the Government. I am quite in agreement with what my hon. friend has said as to the attitude that should be taken by the Canadian government to the recent offer of the United States government to consider the question of the development of the St.' Lawrence waterways. Without question or doubt, that great project will some day be undertaken; it must be undertaken. That great system of waterways which we have through the St. Lawrence and our great lakes into the very heart of this continent will be, and it should be some day, an enterprise that will be taken up jointly by these 
two governments. Canada and the United States are going to live peacefully together, and it is to their mutual interest to co-operate in a matter of this kind. As I understand the situation, the proposal of the United States does not involve any outlay of money at the present time, excepting in a very small degree. It was rather along the line of getting action started with the ultimate development of this project in the way that I have stated. I certainly believe that that matter should not have been turned back by the Government in the way that it was. They would have been well advised had they met the Washington government half way in a consideration of this enterprise.

I should like again to present, on behalf of the people of Canada, the opinion that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his Government owe an explanation in regard to their decision that the present was not an opportune time to take the matter up. Why is it not timely? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has been to Washington, and he must be of opinion that if there is some way in which we can co-operate, we ought to try to do so. The United States have come to this decision after their experience in connection with the Panama canal, the greatest proposition as regards canalization for the improvement of transportation, that was ever accomplished. The expenditure in that case was much larger than the original estimate; but they went to work and completed the canal, and by reason of their experience and success in connection with the Panama canal, they are determined to improve waterways elsewhere on this continent. They have made an offer, and for the time being the people of Canada are told that this is not the right time to take this matter up. I should like to have an answer from the Government-perhaps the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) will give it-why that offer has been declined for the present. If the question is one of money and the getting of money, I have no doubt that the money immediately necessary for expenditures in connection with deepening the waterways up to the Great lakes can be found by the United States without any trouble at less than four per cent. I imagine the United States Government can get all the money they want for the immediate development of the St. Lawrence waterways at probably 31 per cent, and thpt they would charge us nothing more than that rate.

Supply-Welland Canal
Did they make the same offer in connection with the Welland canal?

That is what I want to know, and that is what the people want to know-whether they made the same offer in connection with the three waterways. All our chambers of commerce in this country are holding meetings and a great international association has been formed for the promotion of this proposal. It involves diplomatic relations and it necessitates correspondence. It involves the President of the United States, who is a man of his word, and who comes to a friendly government, as I believe he takes Canada to be, and makes an offer to us at this time when transportation is a fundamental question in America. We are, however, told in a short answer in this House, that this is not the timte to take up the matter. I hope the Minister of Railways will give us more details about the correspondence and will give some assurance to the people of Canada and at the same time to the people of the United States, that Canada is prepared to consider this question and is ready, at least, to have the proposition laid on the Table, so that the people of Canada and of the United States may appreciate what the proposition is.

I think it is about time that we should stop speaking of great schemes and of spending more money on transportation facilities. We have given the West three transcontinental railways; we are constructing the Welland canal, which requires a great deal of money. I think the scheme of deepening the St. Lawrence should be dropped immlediately for the time being and we should go on with the Welland canal if it is necessary to finish it at an early date. If we had not spent so much money on that canal, we should discontinue it; but from what I can gather from the minister, he is obliged to go on in order to take care of the work that has already been done. As regards this great scheme of deepening the St. Lawrence, I think we have spent enough money for some years to come in transportation facilities, and our friends from the West and Ontario should be satisfied. We in the East are satisfied that our friends from the West and Ontario have sufficient transportation facilities for the moment.

During the last few years the work on this project has slowed up very considerably owing to financial
stress and the necessities of the country in other directions, and in that period a great deal of damage has been done to the half-finished work. Now, the minister would be well advised in doing one of two things: he should either stop the work entirely or else go ahead and do it in a businesslike way. What is the use of allowing half-finished work to depreciate? It seems to me to be a piece of absolute folly, as any one will admit who takes a look at the work. I have seen bridge abutments go out and slip down into the canal, and I have also seen the banks slip. The minister will hardly pretend that it is reasonable to spend $25,000,000 on a work of this kind and then leave it in that condition. The thing is too childish to think of.

There is one aspect of the question that occurs to me. I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend as to the desirability of improving the St. Lawrence waterway, I am strongly in favour of that improvement being made as soon as it is possible to bring it about. I think the time will come when it will be absolutely necessary to do this in the welfare of the people of Canada, both from the point of view of the manufacturing centres in the East and from the standpoint of the grain producing regions in the West. I believe that the matter should be looked to very early and earnestly by the Government of Canada. But the question that suggests itself to me is this: Will not the improvement of the Welland canal be better carried on as a part of the whole project that is now under consideration than as a piecemeal operation undertaken by Canada when she is very much in need of money? I have no notion of wanting to delay the completion of that improvement, but I do question the propriety of our proceeding to piece out here and there this particular work while the whole project is under consideration. If it is proposed that we shall enter into this arrangement, as I sincerely hope it is, then would it not be better for us to undertake this work as a part of the whole scheme rather than do it on our own account?

Of course, I am in
favour of the completion of the Welland canal. But I have always thought it somewhat strange that we should have undertaken a work of that character unless we had it in mind to carry it a good deal further. The development of the Welland canal will allow us to bring boats
Supply-Welland Canal

of very great tonnage into lake Ontario from the northern lakes and from lake Ontario into lake Erie, but it is very doubtful in my opinion whether the advantage we shall gain by the completion of that work with the limited amount of service we can get from it justified the undertaking at the commencement unless we had something else in view. My hon. friends from Montreal and the province of Quebec, as well as their newspapers, seem to be afraid that the development of the St. Lawrence is going to be injurious to their interests. To my mind that is a very shortsighted view to take of the project. I confidently believe that that work will be proceeded with before many years, and I venture the prediction that no province in the Confederation will profit more from its completion than the province of Quebec. It will enable them to transport their manufactured goods to the head of the lakes at a cost of perhaps one-eighth of what is charged by the railways to-day. That fact is all that need be stated to men engaged in large businesses in Quebec to convince them that the work will be of great benefit to that province. Such advantages as the manufacturers in the province of Ontario have in the matter of freight rates as against Quebec would be entirely eliminated, for a vessel could load at Quebec and be given the same freight rate as if it were loaded at Toronto. My hon. friends from Quebec and their newspapers enlarge on the cost and tell us, perhaps truly, that we have not enough money to embark upon so considerable a project. Well, as I think has been pointed out before, the Dominion of Canada does not need to raise one dollar to carry out the work. The plan that has been suggested is for the government of the United States and the government of Canada to charter a commission that will render the service at cost, giving that commission power to issue bonds. There can be no doubt that they could issue bonds at 4 per cent for two or three times the amount of money necessary.
At 3i per cent.
At least, what I have stated is the opinion of very eminent men with whom I have talked on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Without government guarantees?
No, both governments would guarantee the bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another thing.

But I submit that the project is of such a character that we should never be called upon to pay anything on our guarantee. I do not know that this is the time to go into the details of the question, but that is the plan that has been proposed, and to my mind it is one that is entirely feasible. The credit of the country would, of course, be involved, but the country would not be called upon to undertake the issuing of bonds at 5 per cent.
Now, with regard to the cost of the Welland canal, I think the problem will be largely solved by the completion of the larger work. The project, as set out in the report which my hon. friends have read, takes the Welland canal as part of the whole undertaking, and the cost of that canal-what we have spent and what is still to be spent-is to be part of the international obligation. That is a very material fact. It means that we go on and complete the Welland canal and make the waterway from the Atlantic ocean to the head of the Great lakes, and all the money that would be spent in completing the canal would be shared by the United States as a part of the entire project. I have been surprised that hon. gentlemen from the West, and the people of those provinces, have not gone into this international project more deeply and shown a greater interest in it than they seem to have taken. It means to them not only getting their grain out at somewhere between eight to ten cents a bushel less than it costs to transport it to the seaboard to-day, but all the manufactured goods that they take into the western provinces would share equally in the lower freight rates. And to my mind it is not to lower tariffs that my hon. friends from the West must look for relief, but to lower transportation costs.
Both.

Well, you have a long way to go before you will get tariff reduction, as I think you must be convinced by what has happened this session. But, Sir, you have not very far to go to get the other, and personally I regret that the Government did not at least show more sympathy with the approaches made to them by the authorities of the United States than the newspaper reports would indicate. I do not think that there is anything before the people of Canada to-day that will give them greater relief from the burdens they are

Supply-Welland Canal
carrying, and greater advantages for the future development of the country, than the completion of this great waterway. Providence has put in our hands something of inestimable value, and we are letting it lie undeveloped. The time will come when all the railways we have will not be sufficient to carry the traffic from the central and western portions of this country. That state of affairs has already arrived in the United States; that country must have other and better means of transportation for the products of the western and central western states. We are not as congested as they are yet, but we hope that that congestion will come, as it must come with additional population. Therefore it is wise for us to have some vision on a great project of this kind and if we are not prepared to say, "We will look with sympathy into those representations which have been made to us by our great neighbour to the south;" we might at least say, "Whatever we may do in the future, we think this is worth talking about and looking into." But, unfortunately, the Government has not gone that far, and I sincerely regret the course which the negotiations have taken.

I still press the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) for an answer to the very fair question I put to him, namely, to give the House the reason why it is not informed of the policy of the Government in delaying action in this matter. To that I would add this thought. Imagine the relief that would be given to unemployment in this North American continent to-day if the policy which the President of the United States has in view, involving perhaps an expenditure of $300,000,000 or $400,000,000, for the building of a great highway, largely at the expense of the United States, were undertaken. I believe that money would be forthcoming at 3 or 3i per cent. It was not long ago that the government bonds of the United States were saleable all over the world at a price that gave a return of 3 per cent. I believe that day is coming back again, I predict that when the building of that international waterway is undertaken all the money will be found in the first place by the United States at 3 per cent, and that we will not be charged any more than that rate for our proportion of the capital outlay. In that way relief will be given to unemployment, and, most of all, relief will be given to transportation.
With regard to the opposition to this project from Montreal, the people of that city
think there is only one solution of 4 p.m. the transportation problem-by rail. There is, I contend, a better solution of that problem by developing our waterways and so enabling sea vessels to reach the upper lakes. Montreal's vision is distorted because it cannot see any other solution of the transportation problem, and this rail solution would perhaps be controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, of Montreal. Now, that company is in the ocean business and has large fleets of its own, but it would not like to see its vessels sent up to Duluth, Port Arthur and Fort William in competition with its railway. What is holding back this great undertaking? The railway interests of Canada and of the United States. But they cannot get by the President of the United States and the farmers' bloc. The President has brought forward this policy and has invited our co-operation-the first time that we have ever been approached by the United States to participate in a great international project. And yet the party that was in favour of reciprocal trade arrangements with the United States is not prepared to co-operate-or at least is prepared to delay entertaining the proposal for a solution of our transportation problem based on seaways as well as on railways.

I am interested in the conflicting statements that have been made in regard to this matter. The member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) has just stated that there would be a saving of from 8 to 10 cents a bushel on grain from the West to Montreal if the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence river were opened up for seagoing boats. I find that in a discussion which took place a short time ago in the Senate a statement was made that it now costs 7 cents a bushel to carry grain from Fort William to Montreal. So how it would be possible to save 8 or 10 cents a bushel when the total cost is now only 7 cents is something that I cannot understand. From information I have received I understand that during last season a private company purchased and placed on the lakes five new boats for the grain traffic as they found the business so profitable. In looking over the report of the International Joint Commission I was struck by some of the information it contains. In the discussion that took place in the House some time ago in regard to this matter I was led to believe that the total cost would be $252,000,000. I have been rather surprised to find that that sum only covers

the cost up to the Welland canal, and that to get at the total cost one would have to add $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 for the widening and deepening of the Welland canal, and that there has already been spent $2,900,000 on what are called the St. Clair flats. These would have to be deepened, as well as the Soo canal, in order to enable great boats to pass from Fort William to Montreal.
I have heard nothing in this discussion so far about great ocean liners from Liverpool going up the lakes to Fort William. I believe that prospect carried considerable weight at one time. In the evidence given before the commission I was surprised to find the statement that it costs three times as much to build a boat for the transatlantic traffic as for the lake traffic; and added to that is the fact, also rather startling, that one of those large boats would carry only about 60 or 65 per cent of the amount of cargo that a lake boat of similar tonnage would carry because of its deeper draught and special form of construction for deep sea traffic. Let me repeat that. A boat that is intended to carry grain from Fort William to Liverpool would have to be built so strongly that it would cost three times as much as a boat of the same tonnage on the Great Lakes. Think what that means in extra cost and overhead charges, and the greater cost in man power. This cost would have to be borne-and would bear interest-up through all these canals. I was also surprised to find that between Prescott and Montreal there are some forty-four miles of canal. It showed me how little I knew of the geography of my own country. The evidence given before the commission would show that a large boat could not pass through these canals at a greater speed than four miles an hour, and there is great danger of them being rubbed against the side, causing considerable damage, and hours delay before they can be released.
Does the hon. member think they could use some of the Canadian merchant marine boats on those canals? It would not be much loss if they were damaged.

I have heard some
rumours about the merchant marine, but I would not like to pass any opinion on that question. One hon. member has said that there would be a saving of 11 cents per bushel on grain passing through the Welland canal, and of 1 cent a bushel pas-

Supply-Welland Canal
sing through the other canals to Montreal, or a total saving of 2J cents a bushel. If we reckon up the interest on the large amount of money required to complete this waterway, and reckon what would be saved even if grain could be , carried for two or even three cents a bushel cheaper,-and that would be near the limit, I believe,-we shall find that it would be a losing game, and that grain could be carried free, through the Welland and Lachine canals for less than the interest on the investment.
There is another matter that should be considered, because I believe some are still of the opinion that we can open up a route between Fort William and Liverpool or London. The great carriers that come across the ocean bring with them a cargo, That cargo at the present time, and for years to come, must be unloaded at Montreal. It is not a cargo for Fort William, and for many years to come Fort William cannot be a distributing point. Think what it would mean for one of these boats to stop at Montreal and unload, and then have to crawl empty, at the rate of four miles an hour, through 44 miles of canal, through the Welland canal, the St. Clair flats, the Soo canal and up to Fort William. Think of the lost time when they could be loading and unloading at the same time, as they must do if they are going to make dividends. You cannot load at one time and unload at another and make it pay.
I am not going to go more fully info the whole question of the deep waterway except to say that much of what has been said, and is believed, is based on information that is not well founded. We have our railway transportation problems at the present time, and great problems they are. While this waterway might result in a slight saving in transportation costs, it would take a certain amount of traffic from the railways. The time may come -I would not go so far as to say it never will come-when this route will be feasible and the Welland canal may pay, but at the present time, I am convinced, it will not pay, and considering that money is so much needed for other things I think it is unwise for the Government to expend this amount of money at this time.
The argument-and it is a very good one -has been made by the minister that much of the work that has been done would deteriorate if further amounts are not spent. But that argument also holds good in connection with several branch lines of railway. I referred to one some time ago, where the farmers were so anxious to have the railway that they offered to build it themselves and pay for it out of the freight. I receive letters quite frequently in regard to this branch line, saying that the farmers are drawing their grain nearly twenty miles, and that it is turned over to the Canadian Pacific rather than to the Government railway.
There is also the plea made on behalf of the unemployed. I think it would be much better if this Government would undertake to build with a part of this money some of the branch lines that are very much needed, and take those who are willing to work in the Welland canal district over the railways free to places where they are required, and bring them back again free. This would be work that would open up the country, and encourage an industry that is not now getting the consideration it should. These branch lines would serve as feeders for the present railways, would be an encouragement to agriculture, would produce freight, and, due to the greater buying power of those who are on the land, would help industry as a whole. On the other hand, I am convinced that if $8,000,000 is spent on the Welland canal this year, the benefit will be so small that very few will feel it. I think the Government would be well advised to reduce this item by one-half and spend the other $4,000,000 where it is much more needed. I do not say, spend it on branch lines necessarily, although I think that is perhaps where the money is most needed, but spent it wherever it is most needed. If there is any industry that is requiring assistance more than the agricultural industry spend it there. Certainly there are many ways in which it could be spent to advantage.
I know there is an inclination to pass this item without further discussion, but it is a large appropriation, and I do not . feel I would be honestly representing my constituency if I allowed it to pass unchallenged. I would just like to ask the House for a little sympathetic consideration. How would this project look to the man-I know this is an extreme case-who in order to keep the sheriff from the door last fall borrowed $400 at 25 per cent interest, and the loan was partly or fully covered by giving in return a Ford car and some other goods. That man has worked hard all his life. How would this undertaking look to him?

I notice an inclination on the part of some people to say, and I have heard it said in this House: You farmers ought to quit grumbling and get down to work. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers are not grumblers. With fair treatment, they are prepared to take their losses and gains without any grumbling whatever, but I can point to thousands of men who know the business of farming, who are slaves to work, and economizing more than they should be compelled to do, who waste nothing, and yet at the end of their year's work find - and this is no exaggeration - that they have not made, one cent. The return they get for their grain in many cases does not pay the cost entailed in securing the seed, sowing the grain, reaping, harvesting and threshing it. Now, I know some will smile and say that statement is surely exaggerated. However, I venture the assertion, that if I could not prove it to be correct in a reasonable length of time, on the authority of hundreds of letters, I would be willing to resign my seat in this House. Bearing that fact in mind, if my seat mate will act as seconder, I am going to move that this item be reduced by one-half, that is reduced to $4,000,000.

I believe this has been
an ill-advised scheme from the beginning. To think of constructing a canal in the middle of this continent, without having the approaches at either end of the same capacity, is most unreasonable. Thirty million dollars have already been spent, which will not be revenue bearing, at least, until about 1930. By that time another $30,000,000 will also be spent, and the interest on that at 6 per cent would meet the cost of carrying the whole of the western wheat crop that goes by this route, clear across the peninsula. I am very much surprised to hear the warm advocacy of this scheme from our friends in Toronto. I believe they see the possibility of deriving more benefit from it than anybody else, and perhaps they are thinking only of their city.
We are thinking of the West.

The greatest surprise of all to me is to hear hon. gentlemen to my right warmly advocate the co-operation of the United States on the ground that this is an international undertaking when, only a few years ago they told us we were not to have " truck or trade with the Yankees " in relation to a scheme that

would have been of international benefit, and revenue bearing from the very beginning. As to unemployment this project will not result in any lasting benefit, even though it may relieve unemployment for the time being. Our unemployment problem will rightly be solved by further* developing some of our natural resources and building branch lines. As one hon. member has already stated these would be revenue producing from the time they were completed; and it would only take a few million dollars to furnish facilities for those in the West who to-day are not only suffering inconvenience, but absolute hardship. My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) has emphasized the unreasonableness of leaving a project like this remain unfinished and to deteriorate year after year. I can point out to him a project started in western Canada over ten years ago upon which $20,000,000 has been spent, and I see an item of $40,000 in the estimates this year to take care of the terminals of that railway only, although the grades are levelling down and the steel is rusting. I certainly oppose this estimate and do so with a clear conscience.
. Mr. MANION: I do not wish at this stage of the proceedings to cause any delay in the passage of the estimates of any branch of the government. I do not think, perhaps, that this is the most suitable time to discuss the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Waterways project, and I do not intend to do so except to offer two or three sentences which will perhaps clear the air a bit. My hon. friend from Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Millar) has said that he did not see where the saving would come from in connection with this enterprise. Well, I am not authority enough to tell him exactly where the saving would come from but the best authorities in the world who have investigated this scheme say it will save anywhere from five to ten cents a bushel on the wheat handled, not only from western Canada but from the western states. Julius Barnes, perhaps the best authority in the world to-day on grain statistics, says in the report from which my hon. friend quoted, that it will save ten cents. Herbert Hoover makes the same statement. Some of the other authorities assert that the saving will be five cents on the wheat coming from the West to-day or at least very much of the wheat -I refer to the proportion which goes down to Port Colborne, or perhaps to some

Supply-Welland Canal
of the Georgian Bay ports, and is there transferred and taken to Montreal. If the wheat does not go by the Canadian route, it is shipped to Buffalo where it is transferred either to the Erie canal or to railway cars and taken to New York. I believe the cost of shipping from the Georgian Bay ports and Port Colborne to Montreal, and from Buffalo to New York, is in the neighbourhood of nine or ten cents. The saving would be there. If wheat could be carried by boat all the way from the head of the lakes to Montreal that would result in a great saving. At present it is transferred at Port Colborne, or Buffalo, or some of these other points, and shipped by rail to Montreal and New York. That is where the saving comes in. My hon. friend made the statement-it was made by other members when this question was up before in the House; the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) made the same statement if my recollection serves me correctly-that the interest on this expenditure was too great. But if the actual saving should happen to be five cents a bushel, if this scheme were carried through, it would mean a similar amount on every bushel of wheat grown in the prairie provinces. Not only that but as my hon. friend knows the price of wheat is fixed in Liverpool for the whole of the western provinces-not merely for the wheat sent to Liverpool-and supposing the saving in the carriage of wheat amounted to five cents a bushel, the total saving on 300,000,000 bushels would mean $15,000,000 a year which would pay the whole interest, as a mater of fact, on Canada's share of the cost of this entire project.

I would like to ask my hon. friend some questions. Is he aware that the Erie canal, which is a strong competitor with us in the carriage of wheat, has a draught of only eight or nine feet? Secondly, would he say positively that the present freight rate is more than seven cents front Fort William to Montreal? My figures are taken from a speech delivered recently in the Senate by Senator Casgrain.

Senator Casgrain is very much opposed to this scheme and loses no opportunity of expressing his opposition. Leaving that aside, in answer to my hon. friend let me say that I cannot give the actual figures, but I know that what I stated is correct. In the very report from which my hon. friend quoted, Herbert Hoover
and Julius Barnes say that the construction of this enterprise will make a saving of ten cents a bushel on the carriage of American and Canadian wheat. However, cut it down to five cents, which other authorities in the same report say would be the right figure. I believe my hon. friend will find that you cannot carry wheat to-day with navigation open from Fort William to Montreal for anything like seven cents a bushel. I may be wrong, but I think I am right, I am quoting authorities from the report of the commission appointed by the two governments. They took up an entire year to investigate this matter and this is their report. I must confess that when I was told that five or ten cents a bushel would be saved I did not believe it; but when the report came out and gave that figure on the authority and as the finding of the commissioners I had no hesitation in accepting it, speaking generally. My hon. friend mentioned the idea of boats coming from Liverpool to Fort William, or to the head of the lakes. I do not think there is very much likelihood of that happening, at least not to any extent. The idea would be this: Wheat would be carried from the head of the lakes to Montreal and there transhipped to ocean-going vessels. There is a type of vessel projected for canal, lake and ocean service, and I am told by competent engineers that the construction of this class of vessel would not cost any more than the building of any other type of boat.
Some of the Canadian Merchant Marine vessels?

I am not referring to the Canadian Merchant Marine. Still, I have enough confidence in Canada to believe that we can build a merchant marine to suit this service. There seems to be a tendency, a continual tendency, to make fun of the Canadian Merchant Marine and at times, to make fun of everything Canadian. I admit many boats of the Canadian Merchant Marine are probably idle at the present time; so are many boats of the private corporations. I do not think there is anything particular to be gained by interjecting uncalled for references to the Canadian Merchant Marine, because it has nothing to do with the matter. The point I was making was that I had been told by competent engineers, one of them living in Ottawa, a representative of Sir Robert Perks, the gentleman who wishes to build the Georgian bay canal. This engineer has been studying the question for some years,
Supply-Welland Canal

and he told me personally that a boat could be built to serve both lake and ocean at little, if any, greater cost than the ordinary cost of building boats for ocean or lake. However, the point I wish to make is that it is not the intention in this canal scheme mainly to have boats run straight across the ocean. They would probably run to Montreal or to Quebec. The saving would be in the carrying without breaking bulk from the head of the lakes to Montreal or Quebec. I do not think the statement of the hon. member from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Miller) should go unchallenged, especially when we have the report of the commission which states the opposite.
I think it is rather an extraordinary proceeding for the Government to have practically refused to discuss this question at all with the United States' government. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has suggested that the reason is the lack of money. I do not dispute that, and I do not argue that the Government should not take any particular stand they choose. That is their right. But it is an unprecedented thing, it seems to me-and some of the Washington papers made a similar statement when the matter occurred-for one government to absolutely refuse to discuss with another government a question of international importance such as this. I do not say this particularly with a desire to criticize the Government, but I think they might be well advised to reconsider the question of discussing this matter with the United States' government. The fact, that they consented to discuss the matter would not by any means tie them up to the proposition, and it would not in any way tie my hon. friends to my left or any of them, to the proposition, but certainly all information on such a subject as this might well be gained by all of us, and certainly by the government in power. So that, I submit, with all due respect to the Prime Minister, that he might well reconsider the stand he has taken on the question and listen to and take part in such discussion, if the opportunity arose, wholly in the interest of getting information for the Government, and for the people of this country. If, after those discussions the Prime Minister chose to take an attitude absolutely opposed to the building of the canal, it is his right, but I do not believe it is in the interests of the Government or of the country for the Government to absolutely refuse at this time, or any other

time, to discuss a question of such great magnitude and importance as this.

We were asked to enter into a treaty, and we said no; that having regard to the magnitude of the matter, the expenditure involved and the importance of the question, we have not had time to consider it. We have not closed the door to discussion.

I am only going by the
Prime Minister's own words. 'He said in reply to a question asked by Sir Henry Drayton:
-"the Government has replied tc the effect that the present is not an opportune moment to take the matter up."

The hon.
member was asking about entering into a treaty, and the reply was that this was not an opportune moment to discuss the question of making a treaty.
But has not the Prime Minister and the Government absolutely refused to discuss the matter at all with the Government of the United States?
