The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) made a similar statement a few minutes ago, and he must have taken it from the words of the Prime Minister, as I did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I laid the correspondence on the table of the House, and I think it was ordered to be printed. I do not know if it has been printed, but if hon. members will read the correspondence they will see that the communication received by this Government from the United States government related particularly to the question of entering into a treaty, and the reply related to the question of the treaty, and the discussion of the matter was not precluded. What I wanted to say particularly was that the Government had not had time to study the report. And until we have time to study the report, it would be unwise to talk about a treaty.

I am pleased to have the Prime Minister make the statement he has made. We drew a wrong conclusion from his words, but the conclusion drawn by me, the hon. member from Marquette, and other members of the House, was

Supply-Welland Canal
drawn from the words of the Prime Minister. I admit I have not read the correspondence, but I took his words in the House. However, his statement now is more satisfactory. I do not dispute it at all, and I believe it better that this information should have been given to us all.

I would like to say a few words on this question before the vote is taken. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) said that he was surprised that the farmers were not interested in a proposal which would save them so much money. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) also spoke in the same strain. They are surprised we are not interested. Well, we are interested, but we are also sceptical. I wonder who the saving is going to be for.
The farmer.
I doubt it. I say that we have spent millions of money on the waterways, and the more money we spend the higher our rates go. There was an increase from 1919 to 1920 of 2i cents a bushel.
Could we get the crop of western Canada out of the country at all, if it were not for the money that has been spent on the waterways of the country?

That is all right, perhaps we could not, but the more money we spend the higher the rates go. Is that saving going to be for the farmers or for the big watered stock companies, such as the Canada Steamship Company?
No. A commission will be appointed to work on costs.

This battle has been fought in this House time and again, year after year, for the control of the rates on our waterways and has been objected to by my hon. members on both sides of the House. They will not allow those rates to be brought under control, as the railway rates have been. A gentleman named Armstrong used to be a member of this House, and I find that, year after year, he brought up this question very very forcibly, and it was always resisted, and there was no control given over these rates whatever. Suppose we do improve these waterways, and we can carry the wheat and goods from the head of the lakes to Montreal so much cheaper, does that not mean that railway rates also will have to be reduced in the East to compete
with that water transportation? And if they are reduced in the East, does it not mean they will be increased in the West to make up for it?
No.
My hon. friend says no, but that is the experience we have been having for years.

Let me answer the hon. member. The hon. member knows that today all of the wheat of western Canada, or at least a large proportion of it,-until very recently 65 percent-went by the Erie canal and New York. I know that to be a fact. The building of these canals would permit that same wheat to go straight down the Canadian route, and there would be a saving. It costs I think in the neighbourhood of 10 to 11 cents to take it from Buffalo to New York. That saving could easily be made on that trip alone for sixty-five per cent of the wheat that is exported from western Canada at the present time.

The hon. member may be correct, but I have my doubts, because I find that the boat freight was 8.6 cents; it is now 11.8 cents all the way from Fort William to Montreal by the boats which we have now. In 1919, the rate was 11 cents, and in September, 1920, it was 133 cents. In October, when our wheat really begins to move and they could do us a service, they increased the rate from 11 cents, as it was the year befpre, to 15i cents, and we have no control over them.
There is something else that I wish to know. There are a few boats running down from the head of the great lakes, boats like the Grant Morden-I have been to Fort William and Port Arthur and I have seen them-that can carry these big loads; but there are only a few. Does the Canada Steamship Company intend immediately to scrap all the boats it has at present which can go through the Welland canal and all the way to Montreal, and replace them by these big boats which can carry 500,000 bushels? I do not think so. Until the canals at Montreal are finished, I can see no good in this Welland canal project, because the boats which now can go through the Welland canal can now go through to Montreal. When you get your larger boats through the Welland canal, you have to build bigger elevators at Kingston and Prescott, transfer elevators, or the scheme is of no value at all. If my hon. friends would move that the whole
Supply-Welland Canal

item be cut out except just what is needed to keep the canal from falling into decay, I would vote with them. I will vote with them as it is; but I think they do not go far enough. I think the whole proposition was a mistake, as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) says, in beginning in the middle a scheme of this kind. At this time, when economy is needed, what is the use of talking about economy and then voting millions of dollars for a proposition like this? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), last night, I think, had some matter on which he could spend $2,000,000 of this very money, and I would like to see the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) do what has been suggested without our having to take a division on the question. The Government should practice economy as well as preach it.

In the first place, I
think the Government used very good judgment when they said that the time was not opportune to enter into any agreement with the United States. We have heard a great deal about some people having a vision of a greater Canada, and some people think they can see further ahead than others. Some years ago we had that class of men in British Columbia, and they told us about some railways that were needed. They also told us that the proposition would not cost the taxpayers of British Columbia one dollar; but when it was completed, the taxpayers of British Columbia have had to foot a bill of over $40,000,000, and that railway is . not making a cent. It started nowhere and it ends nowhere. We have too many people working up propositions in their own interest and not in the interest of Canada as a whole. I claim to know a little about steamboats, and there is in my mind a question whether ocean steamers of large tonnage would ever come up through the St. Lawrence canal when completed. If we take insurance and other things into consideration, I do not think it would pay them to do so. As an hon. member has stated, ocean steamers are built much heavier; the captains and engineers get higher pay; they have to carry a larger crew than would be required on the canal travelling at a low speed. While those boats were on the ocean, they would go at twelve or thirteen knots an hour, whereas, through the canal, they would have to go at three or four knots an hour. The wages of the crew and other expenses 'Mr. Sales. 1
including the interest on the investment in the boat, would go on just the same. The heavy machinery and other things would add to the expense. I question, therefore, whether the proposition would ever be used to the extent some people think it would. I do not think, with the amount of burden that this country is carrying at the present time, this proposition should be given any consideration at all. We are not sent here to consult with the United States and to consider their propositions; we are sent here to represent the people of Canada, and to work in their interest.

Before I
can intelligently vote on the amendment and on the resolution, I shall have to have some more information from the minister. I will ask my question first. What would be the probable cost to the Dominion were work discontinued on this project and it were allowed to stand over for a year or two? I should like to refer very briefly to the amendment and to the resolution. I should like very much to support the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Millar), but I fear that it is subject to the same criticism as was offered against the project generally,-it starts in the middle and does not go anywhere. If the principle is right, I think his amendment should have read to delete the entire thing except such as would be required to prevent loss, or else to go ahead with the thing in a whole-hearted manner and complete it. When the debate started, I had an open mind on this subject, although I was probably a little inclined to cut it out in the interest of economy, because I think economy is demanded at this time. I was, nevertheless, very much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol). I am not able to judge as to the correctness of his figures, I should like to have them confirmed. If those large boats, as he states, can, by this expenditure, go through the Welland canal, unload at Prescott instead of at Buffalo, transfer their cargoes to barges which can cheaply be carried down the St. Lawrence river and unloaded at Montreal, that is a very desirable thing. The other day we had it on informrtion given us by the Chairman of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners that 135,000,000 bushels of wheat passed through that port last year-I think the quantity was quoted by an hon. member a short time ago as 115,000,000 bushels; but my recollection is that the correct quantity is 135,000,000

Supply-Welland Canal
bushels,-about 65 per cent of which was Canadian wheat. If - e can, by a development of this sort, bring down a larger volume of wheat from Buffalo to Montreal and develop the port of Montreal rather than the port of Buffalo and, consequently, New York, that would he a very desirable thing. But it involves a considerable expenditure; it involves transfer houses at Prescott, while we already have transfer houses at Port Colborne and elevator space at Buffalo. Another hon. member, who represents, I think, one of the Toronto seats, referred to the return cargoes. In my opinion, that argument has very little weight, because, if I am correctly informed, the return cargo carried by those boats is principally coal from the Pennsylvania mines to western Canada. There is practically no heavy package freight going from Montreal up through the lakes to western Canada. Freight which goes that way has to go mostly over the railways.
Why?

I suppose
from the very nature of it; it is not bulky like coal. I do not know of any freight of any considerable volume going up the lakes to the western prairies.

Why could the boats
not take package freight?

Because package freight is a freight that has to be speedily carried through, and boats take a longer time to do that. The freight rate is not the consideration which it is on bulk commodities, on such heavy stuff as ores, lumber and coal. On the whole, I think that ultimately this entire project, in the interests of this country, must and will be carried through. I want to see it carried through for the development of the eastern ports and the various facilities which we have built at enormous cost. But at the present time, when the need for economy is so great and there are other projects requiring huge expenditures, when, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) under the best circumstances possible we can scarcely hope that our revenue will be equal to the expenditures that are to be made during the present year, unless it is necessary to spend a large amount of money in order that expenditures already made may not prove futile, I think we shall be very well advised if we cut out these expenditures for some considerable time. I cannot vote for the amendment, because it begins in the middle and goes nowhere; but
for a reduction in the entire amount I shall be glad to vote.

This whole
matter was gone into very thoroughly by the department. We fully investigated the possibility of shutting down the work, and we have found that if we abandoned operations for two years it would involve a loss in depreciation and deterioration of between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000, to say nothing of the claims which the contractors would naturally put in for such work as has already been done. It must also be remembered that the five sections must be finished as nearly as possible about the same time. The only way you could reduce the vote by $4,000,000, would be to stop the work on one section. That would mean that you would finish four out of five and be unable to use them at the proper time. I can assure hon. gentlemen that we have gone into the matter very thoroughly, and while the members of the Government are as anxious as anybody else to avoid all unnecessary expenditures, we are asking for this vote only because we are convinced that it is absolutely in the best interests of economy.
I understand from the minister that the country would suffer a loss of between five and six million dollars if we postponed this work for two years.
Yes.
Then we had better make the best of a bad job.
Has the minister been over this work personally?

Yes, I have been over it with the engineers. We spent days discussing the matter with the chief engineer, and went thoroughly into the whole thing. We have not rushed things in any way, nor are we asking for this vote without the most careful consideration. We believe that it is in the very best interests of the country to spend this money.

In view of all the statements that have been made I think the mover should withdraw his amendment. It is quite obvious that the reduction from $8,000,000 to $4,000,000 does not give expression to any principle. It gets us nowhere, and I do not think the committee should accept the amendment. I do submit that under all the circumstances, the mover should withdraw it.
Supply-Rideau Canal

I do not rise to criticise the estimate at all, because I agree with the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Johnson) that the minister having been quite convinced that it is necessary to go ahead with this work in the interests of economy, it would be unwise to reduce the vote. I do want to suggest to; the minister, however, that he be consistent in all respects, and give to the various railways that are now half constructed the same consideration that he is giving to this particular matter. We have several miles of railway partly built in the West, and if the minister thinks it is in the interests of economy not to postpone the work under this vote, he should, I think, take the same view in regard to those railways and carry to completion the work in connection with them. The grades have already been built, and I would urge that he seriously consider the advisability of completing those lines.

In view of the fact that some of my statements have been contradicted, I should like to read an extract from a speech of Senator Casgrain. Some hon. members have referred to the fact that he was opposed to the project. If I might do so I would quote some remarks of his.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member would be out of order in quoting from the Senate debates of this session.
Amendment negatived.

Item agreed to.
Trent Canal-construction and betterments, $240,000.

How much
remains unexpended of last year's appropriation?
The amount voted last year was $339,000, all of which was spent.

Item agreed to.
Rideau Canal-construction of storehouse at Ottawa, $4,000.

I do not offer any criticism of this vote, nor am I moving to reduce or to strike it out. I see that on the next page there is a vote of $25,000 additional for the Rideau canal. Placed in such financial straits as we are, it is of course desirable that we should eliminate all expenditures that are unnecessary; and I submit that the minister should immediately decide to part ownership with the Rideau canal. It is as idle

as a painted ship upon a painted ocean; economically it is absolutely useless. It handles not one single cent of traffic, although it is true that a few cart loads of sand are carried through it. I do not know what it costs to carry on the Rideau canal, but probably it takes a considerable sum. I should like to see the minister decide before twelve o'clock to-night utterly to abandon this canal, and hand over to the city of Ottawa the greater part of it, retaining the lower part for railway purposes. I do not suggest that we should strike out this item or the item on the next page, but I certainly do not think that there is any justification whatever for the further retention of this canal. The amount of the vote is small, it is true, but it could as well be expended in purchasing soap bubbles as in further operating the canal, and I hope the minister will rise and say that next week he will advise the city of Ottawa that he is prepared to donate the canal to them for the purpose of beautifying certain sections of the city, retaining the lower part, as I say, for railway purposes.

I would
judge from the remarks of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that in his opinion the Rideau canal is limited to that part of the waterway adjoining the city of Ottawa, and that that is the reason why he would present it to the city. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the point raised by him is much more serious than perhaps he appreciates. The Rideau canal was built by, and at the expense of, the British government and was presented to Canada upon an undertaking by our government that it would be maintained as a canal. So I feel that it would be impossible for the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Kennedy) to act upon the hon. member's suggestion.
My hon. friend surely does not mean to contend that the British government would expect us to carry out that obligation now in view of changed conditions?

I would at least feel that it was an obligation on the part of the people of Canada that should not be decided by the minister inside fifteen or twenty minutes as suggested by my hon. friend; I would think there should be a conference between this Government and the British government before any action is taken as proposed by him.

Supply-Rideau Canal
Was not the canal constructed for military purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No doubt that was the underlying consideration.

I presume
that the British government one hundred years ago was influenced largely by military considerations in building this canal. But there is no doubt the canal was built at a very great cost, extending as it does from the Ottawa river here to lake Ontario at Kingston, considerable engineering difficulties having to be overcome, boats being raised 200 feet out of the Ottawa river by lockage between here and the height of land and then being let down 168 feet into lake Ontario. I am not urging that from the strictly commercial stand-
5 p.m. point there may not be something in what the senior member for Halifax suggests, but the canal has been operated since 1828, and the items in these estimates are surely not of sufficient importance to call for the offhand decision suggested.

I felt so
sure of my ground that I thought my suggestion could be carried out instantly. But I will qualify that and say we might take a few days or a few weeks to put it into execution.

My hon.
friend is entirely mistaken when he says that the canal is of no commercial advantage to the people of Canada. The canal is of very great commercial advantage to the people who live along its banks.
Is the commercial advantage commensurate with the cost to the people of Canada?

I am speaking of the advantage to the people who live along the canal. Since the question of transportation has been a live issue in federal politics we have heard arguments not only in favour of maintaining but of constructing railway lines into territory where there was no suggestion that the traffic returns would justify the cost of construction.

Not from western
Nova Scotia.
I am not talking of Nova Scotia. We have here a means of transportation that is of very great convenience to the people whom it serves.

I would be very glad to be informed about that. I understood that there was practically no business carried on through the canal, with the exception of a little sand brought down to Ottawa from a point a few miles up the river.

Well, my
hon. friend has not been properly informed. I am quite free to confess that the traffic upon the canal has been very seriously interfered with by the construction of the Canadian Northern Railway along the south shore of the Rideau lakes. Prior to the advent of the railway the canal served all the villages and settlements between Ottawa and Kingston, and even yet boats ply to and fro. I am not prepared to say that the traffic would justify the government of Canada or any one else in the construction of this canal as an original enterprise; but we have the canal there, and if after having constructed locks which make the waterways altogether different to what they were in a state of nature we abandon this canal we would at once place the people who live along its banks at a serious disadvantage. The canal is of very great use to those people and they should not be deprived of the service they and their predecessors have enjoyed since 1828. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the freight traffic or any other remuneration that the government gets would justify maintaining this canal, but I do think my hon. friend has an exaggerated idea of its cost of maintenance. It is a splendidly built canal, and if my hon. friend has not gone over its whole course it would do him good to do so, for he would see a wonderful piece of engineering and would pass through the most picturesque part of Canada-a part exceeding in natural beauty the Thousand Islands that we hear so much about. In a word, my hon. friend has suggested something which should not be entertained by the Government.

When I came down to Ottawa as a new member I naturally wanted to get busy, and one of the first matters I inquired about was the cost of the Rideau canal, which was suggested to me from noticing that repairs were being made to the locks here. I therefore consulted the Auditor General's reports to find out the cost of this canal for the last six years. I am not much accustomed to going through these reports, but my figures are as nearly accurate as I could make
Supply-Rideau. Canal

them. I found that during the past six years we have paid for the upkeep of this canal in salaries and repairs a total of $1,205,534.66. The revenue derived from it in the same period amounted to $40,798.63. Being interested in the matter I put a question on the Order Paper-
What was the revenue derived from?

I presume from tolls.
Mr. STEWART Lanark): There are no tolls charged on the canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The revenue was from water-powers probably.
There are developed water-powers on the canal.

As I was saying, I also put a question on the Order Paper, but the answer, I confess, does not mean much to me. This is my question, which will be found on page 734 of Hansard:
How many vessels and what tonnage passed through the Rideau canal during each year since 1915?
The answer will be found on the same page, but I shall not read the figures as they can be very easily referred to by hon. members. Those figures convey no idea to me because I do not know what was the nature of the traffic. As the season opened up I saw that a considerable amount of work was being done on the canal here, but I question very much if, apart from this end of the canal and possibly a few other limited sections, very much traffic is going on.
When the hon. member for Halifax made the suggestion that it be presented to the city of Ottawa, it occurred to me offhand that that was just the thing to do with it. I am not certain that the figures given by the hon. member for Lanark as to what this canal has cost are absolutely correct. I was out at his town of Perth the other day. It is situated at the head of that famous ditch, as we used to call it; we heard of it back in the elections of 1896.
I was interested to know just what that canal looked like, and what it was being used for and from the information I could gather I would suggest that the Tay canal be presented to the city of Perth. I confess after seeing that canal in the town of Perth, some of my prejudices were removed. While there was no traffic on it to any extent, there is a basin and some docks, and no doubt it is a very beautiful thing for the town, but it is absolutely 
useless from a commercial standpoint. I believe the Tay canal does help to take away the sewerage from Perth and give the town better drainage. So I would suggest that the Tay canal be presented to the town of Perth. I came across a little item,- it is a trifling sum in the Auditor General's report,-showing that it costs $95 a year to put down, take up and care for the buoys in the Tay canal. I doubt if the canal is even worth that much for commercial purposes. I admit that the Rideau canal for scenic purposes and excursion parties undoubtedly is some value to the people of Canada, but as a commercial proposition I do not think it is worth considering. I would again call attention to the figures. The Auditor General's report shows that for 1916, 1917, 1918, 1919, 1920 and 1921 the people of Canada have spent $1,205 534.66 on this canal. To what extent it would be wise to continue that expenditure in future, I am by no means certain, but certainly it is not a commercial proposition.
I think that some of the work my hon. friend mentions should be charged up to the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and not to the Rideau canal.

I think the figures I
quoted are accurate. If anything, I think be expenditure would be more rather than less.

The hon.
member said that when he was here last March he saw a lot of work being done along the Rideau canal. That work was being done for the relief of the unemployed and should be charged, I think, to the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and not to the Rideau canol. There was a retaining wall built, for instance, to give work to the unemployed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am very strong on the financial situation. I believe that we ought to be economical, but there are cases where it is a mistake, I think, to insist on estimating the value of a certain work in dollars and cents. The Rideau chain of lakes forms one of the most beautiful spots on the whole North American continent. There is no question about that in the mind of anyone who has seen them. The tourists who spend their summers along these lakes bring thousands and thousands of dollars annually to the Dominion of Canada. We often discuss

Supply-St. Lawrence Canal
in this House the desirability of opening up beauty spots in Canada, and it would not be wise, I think, for the sake of a few dollars to close up this one. It has a historic value, to my mind, apart altogether from its commercial value. It was originally constructed by the Imperial government, I believe, for the purposes of defence, and anyone who will take a trip through this chain of lakes and inspect the masonry will discover something that would be a revelation to the modern mason. On several occasions I have given many Americans the trip from Montreal to Kingston, through the Thousand Islands, down the Rideau chain of lakes, through the canal, and down the Ottawa to Montreal again, and although I am very proud of the Thousand Islands and think it a wonderful beauty spot, the Rideau chain of lakes is in a class by itself. We have spent millions of dollars to build the Trent canal, and the great argument in its favour was that it would enable those living inland and farther west up towards Georgian bay a short and quick method of transportation for light draft freight. The Rideau canal affords the same facilities. It' may be that during the last two or three years little freight has been carried over it, but let me point out to the committee that during the war a great many things went wrong. Before that time I know of my own personal knowledge that coal was transported from lake Ontario to points along the Rideau waterway. There are many bright little towns bordering these lakes, Westport, Portland, Smith's Falls, Perth, and many others I could name. These have all been served for years by this waterway, and I would hesitate for the small expenditure involved to give away this waterway that belongs to Canada. The city of Ottawa could not look after it, and this end of the canal would probably be used as a yard for the railway companies if it belonged to the city. The proposition was made to me when I was Minister of Railways that this end of the canal, where it empties into the Ottawa, should be transferred to one of the railway companies, to increase their facilities and allow them to make a tunnel from that point down to the other end of the city. I pointed out that if they would arrange another outlet into the Ottawa that would be just as satisfactory, we would discuss the matter.
As to the expenditure, hon. gentlemen will see at a glance that if we gave up the proprietorship of this waterway tomorrow, we would still be obliged to keep up the bridges over this stream. The committee will see, when we come to the estimate, that quite a large amount of the money expended has been spent on maintaining the old bridges and constructing new ones over this stream, and we should still be obliged to look after them if we gave up the canal. It is a matter that might be investigated, but certainly this House is not in a position to give instructions to the Minister of Railways at this time to interfere with the situation that has existed for many years. The canal is not altogether useless financially, and otherwise it is a great asset to the Dominion of Canada.

If it is the grand summer resort my hon. friend says, and I have no doubt he has stated the facts correctly, has any effort been made to induce tourists to come here? If this is the most picturesque spot on the American continent, let us advertise the fact and get people here and make the canal pay.

Item agreed to.
St. Lawrence ship canal-surveys and investigations, $50,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It might be opportune for me to take advantage of this item to make a statement with regard to the point raised in discussion on the St. Lawrence ship canal. I have in my hand the communication from Mr. Charles E. Hughes, Secretary of State, Washington, which was sent to the British Ambassador on May 17, 1922, and which, amongst other representations, contains the following statement:
The report of the Joint Commission and the accompanying report of the Board of Engineers have doubtless by this time been considered by the Canadian government. I am authorized by the President to state that he favors the negotiation of a treaty to be framed on the basis of the report of the Joint Commission, or such modifications as might be agreed upon, and I should be glad to be informed whether the appropriate British and Canadian authorities are disposed to undertake the negotiation of such a treaty.
The communication was forwarded by the British Ambassador to His Excellency at Ottawa and came before the Government a few days after it was written. The Government's view on the matter was expressed in a report to Council, the essential
Supply-St. Lawrence Canal

part of which is contained in the following paragraph:
The minister represents, in connection therewith, that Your Excellencys' advisers have not thus far had opportunity to give to the report of the International Joint Commission and the accompanying report of the Board of Engineers appointed to examine the subject, that careful consideration which their importance merits, and that moreover, having regard to the magnitude of the project and the very large outlay of public money involved, the Government is of opinion that it would not appear to be expedient to deal with this matter at the present time.
The whole correspondence, hon. members will observe, relates to the immediate negotiation of a treaty. This Government deems it desirable to have a careful study of the report made, and possibly further expert opinion obtained in regard thereto, before a final answer is given. There was no intention to preclude further consideration and discussion.
Has this correspondence been brought down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has been on the table for a couple of weeks.

I would like to ask the minister for some little explanation of this item. I am told that a staff of engineers has been employed by the department for some time past making surveys along the St. Lawrence waterways. I merely rise for information, not to oppose the item, but in making my statement I would like to point out that I have learned that the more expensive members of this staff are being retained, and the junior members, or the lower priced men, have been let out. Now, that hardly seems fair especially, as I understand, it has created a certain amount of hardship in connection with the staff. If the work is not to be proceeded with it does not seem to me that it is necessary to retain an expensive staff, especially when we remember that expert engineers are paid as much as $10,000 a year. In view of these facts I would like to have an explanation from the minister.

May I say that this item of $50,000 is exactly the same amount that was in the estimates last year, but under a different heading. Perhaps it will appeal to some hon. members who have argued in the past that the Government have rushed into expenditures that upon consideration might not have been undertaken, if I state it was felt that in so far as the deepening of the St. Lawrence is concerned the department itself, and the Government of the day,

should have every possible information. The engineering staff employed are taking borings and investigating and checking matters up, so that when the issue does arise we will be in possession of first hand information on the matters to be decided. As far as my hon. friend's question is concerned I understand the staff is not larger than is absolutely necessary; there may have been some dismissals, but they were perhaps made for the reason that economy was in the air. I am told by my department, and I have every reason to credit what they tell me, that we are not carrying a single official more than is absolutely necessary to give the Government intelligent information.
Is any boring work being done now?
Some borings are being made.
Where?

At the Long Sault rapids.
Soulanges canal-improvements, $214,000.
I notice that the appropriation under this heading last year was $9,500 as against $214,000 this year. I would like to ask the minister why there should be such a large increase?

The increase in the amount asked for this year in comparison with last year is largely on the account of the necessity for re-surfacing the roadway along the canal. The road along the canal is one of the main highways between Montreal and Cornwall. Built at the time of the construction of the canal twenty years ago, it has only been superficially repaired since and is now gradually disintegrating under heavy traffic. It is proposed to re-drain the whole road and reinforce it with macadam and asphalt binder.

What is the
length of the road.

Fourteen miles. We are now under legal liability for the proper maintenance of this roadway, this being a condition when settlement was made for the lands taken for canal purposes, and those situated to the north of the canal were cut off from access to existing roads. We simply have the legal liability, we cannot get away from it. The amount is the estimate that was arrived

at by the engineering department and the work is absolutely necessary at the present time.

How do you
propose to do the work by contract or day labour? .
By contract.

I desire to mention certain figures I have from one township, which is typical of the very large territory which would be served by this railway. I will not give any more figures to prove the facts, except to say that this is typical of a great number of townships. I took the matter up with the Minister of Railways, the deputy minister and the chairman of the Canadian Northern Railway in Toronto. I quite realize the situation presented by the minister, that money cannot be granted for railway extensions this year, particularly in view of the proposed ire-organization of the board. I might say incidentally, that it seems to me high time that some steps were being taken to have that re-organization completed if we are going to get it in time to be of service to us. The officials I have mentioned have given me the assurance, verbally, it is true, very largely, but also by correspondence, which I could read but would prefer not to, that this branch to which I have referred is recognized as most important, and having one of the first claims. This information was given to me in correspondence from the department and also by the minister and the chairman of the board of the Canadian Northern verbally. I have taken their word. I ask one further concession which I think the people of that country are entitled to and which will not cost the Government anything. I refer to the location of the branch line. It was delayed two years owing to some difference of opinion over the location of the three surveys going through the country. I asked the minister, I think in April, if he could assure me that the location of this railway would, at least, be definitely settled during the present year. It will make a great deal of difference to the people in that locality, if they can know just where this railway is to go when funds are available for it. Seeing that that was a verbal communication and that it was very important to me, I rather think I endeavoured to steal a march on the minister. I do not know whether I succeeded or not. I acknowledged that verbal report in writing, in order that I might have the record for my file. I wrote the minister this letter on April 26:
Dear Sir,-I wish to give you written expression of my appreciation of your verbal promise of Monday that you would undertake to see

Supply-Railways and Canals
that the location of the Bengou&h extension of the C.N.K. is definitely settled during the coming summer.
While of course, in view of the imperative necessity of early construction of this line, assurance of such construction would be more welcome, the assurance that the location will be definitely settled during the present summer will give some measure of encouragement to the settlers along that line.
I may add that representations of the most decided character continue to reach me.
That was on April 26, and I thought the matter was settled then. On May 2,
I received a letter from the department, and I will read the last sentence which is as follows:
It is the intention that, when the new board of directors is appointed, they will go into the matter of branch lines very thoroughly, and, no doubt, the proposed Bengough line will be one of the first to be considered.
That was not definite enough for me, so I replied, and on the 23rd of May I received a letter which again made me sceptical. The minister, I am sure, will pardon me if I say that this letter from his department on the 23rd of May appeared to me as being evasive. I wanted that promise very much, so I wrote him again on the 25th of May.
I wish to read this letter, and then I will ask the minister to tell me whether he intends to carry out his promise or whether he recognizes it. This letter was written on May 25 to the Deputy Minister of Railways :
Dear Sir,-Replying to yours of April 5th, again setting forth the attitude of the Government towards branch line extensions and stating that it is the intention of the Government to submit the whole matter to the new board of directors, when such is appointed, I quite agree with you that such action should be taken. Permit me to say, however, that in my opinion, the Government cannot thus entirely avoid all responsibility in the matter.
Promises have been made in years past on behalf of the government of Canada, that such lines would be extended at the earliest possible date, and it makes no difference what political party may be in control, the government of Canada is still the government, and must be responsible for any contract entered into, or promises made on behalf of the Dominion.
I fully understand from my frequent interviews with yourself, the minister and the president of the Canadian National, that these lines cannot be built during the coming year. I have, however, distinct recollection of the promise of the Minister of Railways, and by Mr. Hanna that, recognising the importance of the Bengough extension, it should be one of the first to have consideration when construction work is again commenced, if they have anything to do with it. I further have the verbal promise of the Minister of Railways that the location of this line will be definitely settled during the present summer.
While conceding, under present circumstances. that the line cannot be built during this
year, I still rely on the promise of the minister and of the President of the Canadian National Railway that this Bengough line will be one of the first to receive consideration and that the location will be definitely settled during this summer.
It is on those two points that I would like a word from the minister.

I think, perhaps, my hon. friend has answered himself, because I gather, from what he has said in that letter, that he still relies on the Minister of Railways and the president of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. I say again that this shall be one of the first extensions that shall receive the consideration of the new board. I understand that the delay in building the line was largely because the people in that locality could not decide where they wanted the line. There were two factions; one wanted it to run in one direction, and the other in another. As I told my hon. friend when he called upon me, the matter of locating a line by the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways will not be at the whim of the people of the particular district, but rather it will be located where it is essential in the interest of the people of this country.

I know this difficulty existed; but the local difficulty has been done away with, I think, almost entirely by conference of the people concerned. People have money invested in that locality. Only two or three days ago I received a letter from a gentleman in Montreal, who has a farm along the line, and he does not know what to do with it until the location is settled. I quite agree with the minister that, when the people have a difference as to the location of a line, the Department of Railways or the board must take the responsibility. I am quite prepared to accept that. The thing I wish to know is whether we can get this location settled during the present summer, so that people will know what their investment is and whether they will stay on and wait for the railway. They are going out now by hundreds.

I have no doubt the hon. member will get the decision this summer. This is a matter which the board must decide; but I appreciate the importance of the extension, and I cannot for the life of me see any reason why they should not settle this summer where the location shall be. I certainly will bring

Perhaps the minister will tell the committee and the country when we are likely to have the appointment of the new railway board, and when the work of consolidation will be undertaken.

That is a matter which the board of directors will have to decide. As they will be railway men and men of experience who will acquaint themselves with conditions throughout the country, I have no doubt branch lines will be built where most needed in the public interest. ,

I think this is a fitting opportunity to bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) and the Government as a whole, the question of the ridiculous incongruities which exists as regards legal costs. Some time ago, I moved for a return of fees and costs paid to barristers and solicitors of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and in going over the return, which is only partly here, I find that different departments of government are paying different amounts of fees. For instance, I find that where a man is asked to advise on a claim to property, that is to say, to search the title to the property, make an abstract of title and so on, he probably puts in an account of $25 or $30, which I consider to be a very reasonable amount, as he has drawn up a deed and so on. But this is very often taxed by the secretary of the Department of Justice down to the sum of $18 or $20. On the other hand, I find that governments 
have been prone in the past-I do not blame the last government any more than the present Government-to differentiate as between solicitors, whereas the bar societies of the respective provinces to which these gentlemen belong do not recognize a difference. For instance, regarding tthe Grand Trunk arbitration, the Government of Canada paid one gentleman from the province of Nova Scotia over $27,000. This man received fees of $150 a day; he also received $20 a day for living allowance and a sufficient amount to pay his fare wherever he was going. He is not a poor man by any means; but the government, at the outset of the arbitration, advanced to that man $12,000 for the purpose of carrying him on. That is quite a good advance to give a man, particularly when he only had to go from Halifax to Toronto and Ottawa.
Who is he?

Mr. Hector Maclnnes K.C. of the city of Halifax. I only want to call a spade a spade. When I see other lawyers from Nova Scotia being paid $30 a day and expenses for work that they have come to Ottawa to do on behalf of the government of the country, I submit that it is absolutely unjust and unreasonable to give Mr. Hector Maclnnes or any other solicitor from Nova Scotia $150 a day and $20 a day expenses.
Was he a candidate in the last election?
Yes.

I do not know; the members of the Government will probably tell you that.
Did that gentleman have something to do with the vote overseas in the 1917 election?
I think so.

Not out of the public treasury, though. Now, I protest against a system of this kind. I know these two members of the Bar in Nova Scotia, neither of them a political friend of mine-they are both Conservatives, I may say-who came to Ottawa and did some work for the government. One man did a lot of hard work and received $30 a day, the other man.

The same thing exists in the engineering department, and it is time that the people of this country got a fair accounting and had things run in a business way. To-day the citizens of Canada are crying out, in the words of Revelation, " How long, O Lord, how long?"

Before the House rose at six o'clock the Minister of Agriculture stated that he would make a statement to the House regarding what he had said about the chairman of the Railway Commission, and before proceeding with my remarks I should like to hear that statement made. It might not then be necessary for me to speak.
The people of western Canada are very much dissatisfied with the Railway Commission as at present constituted, and they were, I think, greatly interested in the statement the Minister of Agriculture was reported to have made in his campaign address which, I believe, was to the effect that he would have Mr. Carvell removed from the board. As the Minister of Agriculture has not yet made his statement on that point, I wish to give to the committee some reasons why he should persist in carrying out his promise to the electors of Regina.
When the Railway Commission was sitting in Calgary on April 18, 1921, the chairman is reported to have said to Mr. Wood and Mr. Brownlee, when they attempted to present a statement from the United Farmers of Alberta regarding existing freight rates, that there had been a misunderstanding and that the only evidence which the commission would hear would have to be in relation to the equalization of freight rates between the East and the West. Mr. Brownlee and Mr. Symington both protested against that attitude on the part of the chairman, but he was very obdurate, and although he finally consented to hear Mr. Wood, he warned

him that the evidence he was submitting would not be considered unless it had a direct bearing on the equalization of freight rates as between the East and the West. The following day the commissioner addressed the Canadian Club at a luncheon in Calgary, and in the Daily Herald of April 19, he is reported as saying:
"A healthy railway system is just as necessary to the country as sunshine and rain, and without it the West would still he left to the Indian and the buffalo. It is not pleasant to have a man like H. W. Wood, President of the U.F.A. make the statement, as he did, that he had no faith in the railways, and that because the rates on grain have been increased the railways are no good," The speaker paid that he liked and respected Mr. Wood, but that he was a man of one idea, a thing he admitted himself. He was working for the farmers alone, while the Railway Board were in such a position that they had to consider justice for everybody, not one particular section.
"I don't think that a man like Mr. Wood is entitled to very much credence," said Mr. Car-vell. " I would far rather take the opinion of the average business man who is vitally affected by railway and freight rates and let him be the judge.
Now, what I would like to ask the minister is this: Does this country pay the chairman of the Railway Commission a salary of $12,000-I believe that is his salary, if not, I stand to be corrected- for the purpose of travelling around Canada and telling people that he would put no credence in the word of a man who was working for the farmer? Do they believe that we should have a different status in this country for a farmer than for a business man? I would like to point out that I think the farmer is more vitally interested in freight rates than is any ordinary business man. The ordinary business man adds the freight that he pays to the cost and he charges that to the purchaser of his goods. The farmers' price is set at Fort William and the freight is deducted from that price.
I thought the price was fixed at Liverpool?

Well, Liverpool; it does not make any material difference as far as I can see. When I sell my grain I know it is always quoted at a certain price f.o.b. Fort William. I think it would not be out of place if the minister would give us his opinion in regard to this matter-whether we should continue to pay this salary to a man who travels around this country making such statements as that. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) addressed a meeting in Regina on November 16 at which the Prime Minister, the then leader of the Opposition (Right Hon. Mackenzie King) was present. Speaking of the necessity for reduction in freight rates Mr. Motherwell said:
He would expel Mr. Carvel,1 from the Board of Railway Commissioners if for nothing else, but for the improprieties which he has been committing in addressing club dinners throughout the country and trying to justify existing rates.
I would like to have the Minister of Railways answer this question, if he will be good enough to, and then I think this item should be allowed to stand until the Minister of Agriculture is present and reads us a statement, which he offered to do before we adjourned for dinner.

In answer to what my hon. friend has said I am sure he needs no assertion that the Government has not instructed the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners to go through the country making the statement that he had no faith or belief in what was said to him by farmers. My hon. friend will readily understand that no government would issue such instructions. As far as the chairman of the Railway Commissioners is concerned, the position is one of a semi-judicial character, and there must be a way under the rules of the House to lay a charge if such is warranted. I am not sufficiently conversant with the act to express an opinion, but I believe there must be some other way of dealing with the matter than the one proposed by my hon. friend when he asks that the vote for the salaries of the staff be allowed to stand over for the time being. I think this item is one which concerns the whole department, practically, and I think it is only fair and reasonable, at this period of the session, to ask that this item be passed. If my hon. friend has any charge to make against the chairman of the board I have no doubt that a means will be found to enable him to do so. The salary of the chairman, I may explain, is not included in the item under discussion.

I think that at this stage we are entitled to a declaration from the minister in regard to the policy that is proposed to be inaugurated in respect to this matter.
