I think the wording of this resolution is comprehensive enough, and the amount involved large enough, to justify me in speaking on a matter which I have been waiting for some little time to bring to the attention of the House. I have reference to the Hudson Bay Railway project. Earlier in the session I placed a notice of motion on the Order Paper in connection with this matter, but in deference to the wishes of the minister, on the day
Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.

that I expected to take it up I allowed it to stand; and as private members' day has now passed I have been waiting for an opportunity to bring the subject to the attention of the Government. The question I refer to is the consideration of the report of the Senate Committee in regard to the navigability of the Hudson bay and the fishery resources therein, and also in regard to the ports and railway. On the 23rd of April, 1920, the Senate of Canada ordered that a special committee of the House be appointed to take evidence and report upon these matters. The order reads:
That a special committee of twelve of this House he appointed to take evidence and report at this session upon the navigability and fishery resources of Hudson bay and strait, and of the character of the ports of said Hudson bay with regard to their fitness as railway terminals, and that such committee shall have power to call for persons and papers, and that the said committee do consist of the honourable Messieurs Bostock, Casgrain, Dandurand, Daniel, DeVeber, Fowler, Lougheed (Sir James), Michener, Schaffner, Sharpe, Watson and Willoughby.
This matter has been a live, burning question in the West for very many years. In fact, it has been discussed on the public platforms in that part of the country for over 40 years, and I have personally heard it so discussed for three quarters of that time in Saskatchewan. The people who discuss it believe earnestly in the feasibility of the project and are looking forward to the time when the matter will be brought to a successful conclusion. Some years ago it was so prominently before the minds of the people of Canada, and its success was so apparent, that both political parties adopted it at that time as part of their policies. During the discussion of this subject last year the views of the leaders of both the old parties in this House at that time were placed on Hansard, so that I need not repeat them on this occasion.
What has Hudson Bay to do with the item before the committee?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that the Minister of Railways intimated in committee on a previous occasion that, with the consent of the committee, the question of the Hudson Bay Railway might be discussed on one of the last items. If there is no objection, therefore, the hon. member (Mr. Knox) may proceed.

That was absolutely the understanding. When the estimates were before the committee on

a former occasion we passed an item in regard to the Hudson Bay Railway on the assurance that hon. members might discuss that subject when the last item was before the committee. This item therefore affords the hon. member an opportunity to take the matter up.

Tyrell spent one winter at a station in Hudson strait taking observations for the Canadian government and also looked over the country from The Pas to Churchill on behalf of a company who had some intention of building a railway in that part of the country-a scheme which was afterwards abandoned. He had no hesitation in saying that no difficulty whatever would be found in extending the railway to Churchill. It is the opinion of this committee that the Government would be well advised if before expending any more money on the harbour works of Nelson they were to appoint a committee of expert engineers and railway builders to examine the route to Churchill and ascertain whether or not it is really possible, as the Messrs. Tyrell say, and what would be the cost and advantage of making Churchill the port and terminus of the Hudson bay road rather than Nelson.
In the meantime, the laying of the rails could be completed to Nelson, and that port could be used for the present in its present state.
While no one was able to speak with certainty as to whether the cod fish were plentiful in the bay or not, there is no doubt as to the strait. AL1 the rivers flowing into the bay teem with fish, and walrus and seal are also found in large numbers in the strait. No doubt as soon as the Hudson bay route is established a very large and lucrative fishing industry will be established there. Recent discoveries have shown that the country surrounding Hudson bay is strongly and richly mineralized, particularly gold and copper.
Mr. Stefansson, the distinguished Polar explorer, gave evidence before your Committee. He is a devout believer in the possibility of utilizing what have always been known as the barren lands of the north, and the islands within the Arctic Circle, in the cultivation of the reindeer, caribou and musk ox for the production of meat. He gave evidence as to the splendid quality of the flesh of these animals as food for the people, and as to the cheapness with which it might be produced. He said that the wild lands of the north which have always been looked upon as worthless could carry at least fifty million head of reindeer and ten million head of musk ox, and that the cost of handling these huge numbers would be trifling in comparison with the profit to be made. The effect of this upon the world's food supply would be tremendous, and your committee would strongly recommend that the matter be energetically taken up by the Government.
Your committee makes the following findings upon the evidence adduced before them:-
(1)	That the Hudson bay route is feasible and will probably in time be profitable.
(2)	That the season of navigation under present conditions is at least four months in length and may by reason of improvements in aids to navigation be considerably increased.
(3)	That in the opinion of this committee sufficient care was not taken in the selection of Nelson as the terminus of the railway, and that the Government should not make further important expenditures upon this port without first making a new and thorough examination into the relative merits of Churchill and Nelson as a terminus for the railroad.
(4)	That the waters of the strait and rivers tributary to the bay teem with fish and valuable marine animals, and we believe that the bay is equally well stocked but there has not yet been sufficient data collected as to the extent of the

fisheries of the bay to enable an authoritative statement to be made as to their value.
(5)	That the mines already discovered in the Hudson bay district are of sufficient number and richness to indicate the existence of great potential mineral wealth.
(6)	Your Committee feel that they cannot too strongly endorse the valuable suggestion of Mr. Stefansson as to the cultivation of the reindeer and musk ox, and would urge upon the Government that the Department of Interior be empowered to take hold of this matter, earnestly taking advantage of what has been done in this regard by the United States government.
(7)	Your Committee, although it is somewhat outside the scope of their mandate, cannot close this report without making some reference to the national value of the explorations of Vihl-jalmur Stefansson. He has completely revolutionized our ideas of the region within the Polar Circle. He has demonstrated that it is possible for white men to live and thrive in that northern region though drawing from no other resources than those afforded by the country itself, and he has proven that those lands which were looked upon as barren and utterly worthless will eventually be a valuable asset to Canada. The committee ventuies the hope that the Canadian government will not be unmindful of the great services performed by Mr. Stefansson, whose reward so far has not been commensurate with the national importance of the work he has accomplished.
(8)	Your committee expresses its thanks to vb.e gentlemen who have voluntarily come forward and given valuable evidence upon the important matters under consideration.
(9)	Your committee submit herewith an extract in narrative form of the evidence given before the committee, and beg to recommend that 1,000 copies of this report and the extract of the evidence be printed in pamphlet form for general distribution.
All which is respectfully submitted.
Geo. W. Fowler,
Chairman,
Having given this summary of the evidence, I think it is unnecessary for me to go into detail, but I should like to point out one or two strong reasons, as they appear to me, in addition to those outlined in the committee's report why the completion of the railway and the development of a port on the Hudson bay should be proceeded with.
Since 1918 delegations have waited on the government here on a number of occasions, seeking to have this work pushed forward to completion. I have been a member of some of those delegations, and I might say I was a member of a delegation that waited on the present Government only recently in regard to this matter. Resolutions to the same effect have also been passed by boards of trade in the West on innumerable occasions, and recently the associated boards of trade of Saskatchewan passed a very strong resolution urging that this project should be

Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.
pushed forward to completion. In view of the fact that railway men claim that the average life of a railway tie and the woodwork of a trestle is only seven years, more particularly when the railway is not being operated I would urge that something be done because this work will certainly deteriorate very rapidly if it is not kept in a state of repair. I know that some slight appropriation is set aside for keeping it in repair, but from the fact that 92 miles of grade remains without steel laid, we must draw the conclusion that that grade will undoubtedly be deteriorating, as it cannot be kept in repair. I might point out that steel was laid to that bridge at Kettle rapids on the Saskatchewan river, and for 92 miles between that point and the bay grading has been done but no steel laid. Judging from the conclusions of the Senate committee, I think it would be advisable for the Government during the present summer to have engineers go over the route described by Tyrell Bros., to look into the advisability of branching off at the point they mention south of Nelson and going to Churchill, because from all the evidence submitted we are forced to the conclusion that Churchill is the better harbour of the two.
Naturally I would like to see the project pushed to a conclusion right away, but I know the policy of the Government at the present time is economy, and that is my policy also, but I think a small appropriation could be made to inquire into the feasibility of this route to Churchill. I have discussed the matter with J. W. Tyrell, and he is perfectly confident that there is good railway building all the way to Churchill. He says there is a ridge of gravel running parallel to the coast which has probably been the beach of an ancient sea, and on which there is as fine railway building as could be found anywhere.
I would also point out that wonderful mineral discoveries have been made in that portion of northwest Manitoba and northeast Saskatchewan close to the Hudson Bay railway. Companies, American, British and Canadian, have secured properties there and last year 813 claims were recorded in that district, and during the month of March of the present year 240 claims were recorded, so I think we may conclude that the mineral wealth in that district is well worth looking after. In fact, the district tributary to the railway
has been described as containing enough mineral wealth to pay the national debt. I would not take it on myself to go that far, because our national debt is very large at the present time, but I do know that there are very large deposits there well worth looking after.
I might also allude to the agricultural possibilities in the regions nearest to the bay, which have been settled for many years. Owing to the fact that they receive a reliable rainfall they can depend on a sure crop every year. In my own district, which is some 600 miles distant from the bay, and has been settled for over forty years, there has not been a single crop failure during that time, and from that portion of my constituency known as the Carrot river valley I have information that the amount of grain shipped during the past season ran between seven and eight million bushels. This region is even nearer the bay than the Prince Albert district to which I first referred.
We have lately been hearing something of the possibilities of shipping western wheat and western meat to the European market via the Panama canal. While this may be feasible at the same time it is difficult to believe that it will be profitable because of the length of the haul and the time it takes a ship to get around and to negotiate the canal, and *also by reason of the canal tolls that have to be paid. 1 find from the Panama canal record that last year only 3,500 tons of Canadian wheat passed through the canal, and the tolls amount to something like $1.20 per ton. I thmk, though, that that represents a ton's space as known to nautical men. However, it is a very considerable handicap on the price received by the producer. I would further point out that the distance from Vancouver to Liverpool via the canal is 8,572 miles. The distance from the Hudson bay ports to Liverpool is only 2,926 miles, not much more than one-third of the total distance from Vancouver to Liverpool, and the distance from Montreal to Liverpool is 3,000 miles, so that the ports on the bay have the advantage by some 74 miles even over Montreal. This is something which, I think, should set us all pondering, whether we are interested in developing the great waterways to the head of the lakes, or otherwise. We have here a port distant I would say, only 1,000 miles from the very centre of the wheat producing area of the West. This project
Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.

is something that people out there have been looking forward to seeing brought to fruition years before this, and they are still looking forward to it.
Now, Sir, I would like to point out, in view of the evidence given before the Senate committee and the report founded thereon, that in all fairness to the western provinces this project should be sympathetically considered, and some steps taken on the part of the Government towards completing the railway at as early a date as possible. I know I shall be asked the question; when is that possible? To that I would say that if we can expend between eight and nine million dollars on the Welland canal then, in all justice, let us apply at least one-half of that amount to the completion of the Hudson bay project. By so doing the Government will regain the confidence of the West, a confidence which, I must admit, has been waning of late. It has been shown that the project is perfectly feasible. The climatic conditions are not by any means an insuperable obstacle. Meteorological readings show that the temperatures were higher than those recorded at Winnipeg during the same year. It has been shown that the districts tributary to the railway and the bay carry enough mineral wealth to justify the building of the line. It has also been shown that immense quantities of fish of unsurpassed quality can be secured in this northern region, so located that they are within easy reach of the markets in the centre of the continent. Last, but most important of all, it has been shown that the project would bring the grain and the beef of the western provinces nearer an ocean seaport, and consequently nearer the markets of the world by a distance of 1,000 miles. Surely this should warrant the Government in making a favourable pronouncement on the matter. I have a firm conviction, Sir, that Providence placed the Hudson bay as a natural outlet for the great grain and beef producing areas of this Dominion; and I have enough faith in predestination to believe that it was predestined to carry, at no very distant date, the produce of the western provinces to outside markets. I would most respectfully ask the Government through the minister, to give us some assurance that this project dear to the heart of the western producer, who is so seriously handicapped at the present time, will be sympathetically considered and brought to a successful conclusion at an early date. Such an assurance would do much to 
restore a feeling of confidence on the part of the West, which, as I have already said, is fast ebbing away.
Mr. MOTHERWELL; I would ask my hon. friend if he would recommend the building of the Hudson Bay Railway in advance of the construction of branch lines in the West that are being so earnestly pressed for at the present time? I would enumerate the following branches: Turtleford to Prince Albert; Bengough westward; Prince Albert straight north; Thunder Hill branch westward, and many others. Is it not a case of giving consideration to the most pressing demands first? The feasibility of the Hudson Bay Railway can only be proved by building it first. The kernel of the whole thing is the matter of priority. What undertakings are the most greviously needed? These branch lines that I have enumerated, and others that could be mentioned, or the Hudson Bay Railway?

In reply to the minister I would like to say that I certainly wish to see the branch lines completed, and I emphasized that fact on previous occasions. As to the Hudson bay project I think there should be an investigation of the merits of Churchhill as a port before any further work is done at Nelson. I have already suggested that that work of investigation should be proceeded with during the present summer. I certainly desire to see the branch lines completed because the settlers in the districts concerned are in serious straits for the want of transportation.

I quite agree with what the member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) has said that it would not be wise at this time to complete the Hudson Bay railway in view of the necessity for the construction of branch lines. I would also like to add my support to the request that he has made that the Government should take steps to decide which is the better port on Hudson bay. The opening of the Hudson Bay railway may seem to be a matter in which the industrial centres of the East are not very much interested, but it appears to me that if they would look into the matter very carefully they would see that the project is one of very great importance to them. They should realize what the opening up of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba means to the East. There was a time I think, when it was said that the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway would not pay for the axle grease, but after the lapse of a few years it was found that the construe-

Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.
tion of that railway was of very great value to the East.
Now I wish to touch briefly on a few points in connection with the territory north of where the member for Prince Albert now lives, because he is located pretty close to the northern boundary line of the settled district. Let me refer hurriedly to the southern states and say that there they can grow cotton but they cannot grow corn. A little farther north they can grow corn but they cannot grow wheat. Farther north still, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, they can grow wheat but in the extreme north we find a territory where wheat cannot be successfully grown. Nevertheless they can raise oats, barley and the coarser grains much better than we can farther south. Just a week ago I was talking with a man who had spent a few weeks in Athabaska, which is about 100 miles north of Edmonton. This man was brought up on a farm in Ontario where he spent nearly all his life and he made this statement. He said "The best hundred acres of wheat that I have seen in my life I saw last summer at Athabaska" and as I already stated that district is 100 miles north of Edmonton. He told me of the districts up there where there were large settlements of foreigners. Both men and women worked the land there and were making a great success of it. I was also surprised when he told me of a large settlement of negroes, a fact of which I was not aware. Going over the report to which the hon. member for Prince Albert Mr. Knox) has referred, I say that this country that will grow rich grass, that will maintain millions of heads of caribou and muskoxen, is a country well worth paying attention to. In the report I notice this statement:
Muskox are found as far north as 400 miles from the North Pole.
And they are grass-eating animals. One explorer tells us he saw a herd that he estimated at a million and a half. Another explorer states that he saw a herd that he estimated at three and a half million.
When was that?

Just a few years ago. They are there in millions now. The caribou is practically the same animal as the reindeer, and in the Yukon they are being ranched and herded like sheep. The Americans are making a great success of the business. Stefansson, the explorer, says that the muskox is probably the most
valuable animal in the world at the present time, and that it yields about three times as much wool of as fine quality as the sheep, and about three times as much meat. The Eskimo herd them as they would a flock of sheep. When you come to consider what cheap meat is going to mean in the near future, when you consider that our lands further south have become too expensive for ranching, and that we do not get the rain-fall they do further north, it gives one some idea of that great country north. To put it briefly, the rivers and bays are teeming with fish. I suppose some of you have the idea " Oh, that country is simply a great tract of ice and snow, that will never be settled." Why not? The same explorer states that the snowfall there is very much less than in Winnipeg. I believe the figures are from 25 to 50 per cent of the snowfall in Winnipeg, yet Winnipeg has a population about three times as large as Ottawa. In speaking of the islands of the north and of the coal area, he mentions five large islands in succession, and he states that these islands are all rich in coal, except one. It is well known that coal is very plentiful on the mainland. Some time ago I was talking to a man who had travelled around the country a great deal. He is quite a fancier of pure-bred stock, and he said: "I have never seen at the Chicago exhibitions, or at any of the other large exhibitions, animals better finished than I have seen on the grass in what is known as the Carrot river country." That is, I think, a little east of where my hon. friend from Prince Albert lives. He referred to this district in his address a moment ago.
I wish to add a word in regard to the two ports. I have looked into the matter very carefully, have studied all that I have been able to get hold of in the last two weeks in regard to the two ports, and it seems to me a miistake was made in choosing the port of Nelson. The port of Churchill is protected from all quarters from the wind. It is quite plain from the report that it could be made into one of the best-in fact, the words that were used were one of the best-ports of its size in the continent, with very little expense. I am going to make one further request, and that is this. The American people have taken steps in the Yukon-I do not know just how long ago, but some years ago-to protect their herds of caribou from the wolves. They are animals that do not
Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.

readily protect themselves. Only at certain seasons of the year are the muskoxen in very great danger from the wolves, but the caribou are in danger all the year round. They have engaged a number of rangers, and are paying them from $4,000 to $5,000 each to destroy the wolves in order to protect their great herds of caribou, but the rangers turn the pelts back to the government, and the return from these pelts pays nearly all of their expenses. It may look a long way off, but I would ask the committee to consider, if a farmer had a flock of sheep, and the wolves were destroying those sheep, would he not be ready to take some steps to protect them? These are our flocks. They are a long way off, it is true, but they are ours, and the time will come when we can make good use of them, and I think in the very near future the Government ought not only to take steps to discover which is the best port, and what it will cost to build to that port, but also to take steps to gather further information about that north country, and look into the plan adopted by the Americans for the protection of their great herds of caribou and muskoxen.

I regret to have to trespass on the time of the House in these crowded closing hours of the session, but the Hudson Bay railway is in an important part of my constituency and perhaps hon. members will tolerate me for a short time. I understand the reason for discontinuing this project was the state of our country's finances at the close of the war, and I judge that the same reason obtains as to the further suspension of the enterprise. I am not at all disinclined to give the fullest weight to that consideration. There are times when every part of the world is called upon to restrain itself, even in regard to its legitimate desires, for the sake of the common weal. But I do not think that any part of Canada ought to be asked to suffer from a discriminating economy of any kind, and I would like to see the Hudson Bay railway put into the same category as the enterprises of a similar kind in the eastern part of Canada.
I think there is a tendency in the public mind to entertain a somewhat distorted view as to the relative cost of this enterprise, and consequently as to its demand upon the public purse. Some few weeks ago I was privileged to view the Quebec bridge, and I was told that this enterprise cost something like $25,000,000, and yet there it lay quite comfortably within the

sphere of my unarmed vision, a single link, a golden link if you like, in the long extensive chain of communication between the West and the East. In the Hudson Bay railway, you have, not a single link, but an entire system of communication between the great prairies of the West and a whole hemisphere; that is it opens up the prairies to trade with the Atlantic and every shore on the Atlantic. By adding less than one per cent of the total mileage of our Canadian railways, you bring the prairies actually to the sea at the mere cost of a Quebec bridge. I think that is putting the matter in the right focus.
I want to say a few words regarding that aspect of the question which deals with the natural obstructions which lie in the way of the completion of this enterprise. As regards those obstructions that lie overland, they have already been accurately measured and completely overcome, so that does not enter any longer into the discussion. The real difficulty begins only at the seaboard, and it must be admitted at once that nature has not very richly endowed the Hudson bay with natural harbours. With respect to Port Nelson, I think the facts are pretty well known already. It seems that nature has left very much to the engineer as regards that port, but in such a way as not to make it impossible for the engineer to make a very workable and successful harbour. I think a fair-minded review of the evidence shows that the advocates of Port Nelson have very much in their support, and I believe they are right in prophesying for that port a great future. It is almost worthy of a great future, standing as it does at the mouth of one of the world's greatest rivers. I am sorry this controversy has been revived at the present time to becloud the issue.
As regards Fort Churchill, it seems that nature has been a little more generous, and that there you have, in a somewhat miniature way, a natural port. It seems, however, from all the evidence that I have read, that Fort Churchill does not possess those possibilities of expansion that might conceivably some day be required. In addition to that, it would require 100 miles of additional railway to reach that port, which lies further north in a more inhospitable climate, and we are told that that railway would have to pass over very difficult ground, in fact, over a morass 30 miles in extent. If that matter could be settled in a satisfactory way, I feel that one would

have to admit that Fort Churchill might be the proper place for the port in this scheme, at least, during its experimental stages. Supposing it was established as a port, and afterwards it was demonstrated to be inadequate, it might even then, when it had to give place to Port Nelson, serve as a subsidiary port especially in times of bad navigation.
It is scarcely necessary, however, to discuss the matter of a port, because the crux of this situation lies in the Hudson bay strait. The whole difficulty with respect to this scheme centres in the Hudson bay strait, where the drift ice from Baffin bay and Fox channel moves backwards and forwards with the tide all the year round and provides a serious obstacle to navigation. I have no doubt that we cannot in any way mitigate the seriousness of the obstruction that there exists to all-year-round navigation; but that it is navigable, there has been no doubt for the last 300 years. Hudson, the famous explorer, entered that strait on his fatal voyage early in July, and since that time we have records to prove that the strait has been navigated from the 5th of June until the early part of November. I think we may assume that the minimum period of navigation-and this is proved almost conclusively by the Senate committee and the evidence given there-for the Hudson bay strait is four clear months of the year. That is the irreducible minimum, therefore; but on the other hand we are told that the Hudson bay strait never freezes over; that with a properly constructed ship you could get through there at any time of the year. So, between these two limits, between the minimum of four months and that larger limit of almost twelve months in the year, you have quite a margin for the operation of modern science as applied to navigation, and he would be a bold man who would set any limit to achievements in that direction. The Senate committee had no less than eight witnesses to show that by modern appliances the strait might be navigated considerably longer and with greater safety than it can 'be at the present time. Having read all the evidence that is available on this aspect of the question, I have to conclude that these obstacles are not such that a born Canadian would willingly admit to be in any way insuperable. Our history is a succession of just such conquests as this enterprise sets before us.
In the history of Canada there have been many enterprises that have seemed absolutely insuperable until they have been re-
Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.
viewed in the light of the possibilities that lay behind them. Therefore, I want to say a few brief words in regard to the incentives that exist to overcome those admittedly serious obstacles. First of all, as regards the Hudson bay itself, this immense inland sea with approximately half a million square miles, deserves, on its own account, a humble connection with civilization. An eloquent member of this House, in the early part of this session, compared the Great Lakes with the Mediterranean sea. With greater truth I think the Hudson bay might be called the Baltic of the North American continent. The differences between the Hudson bay and the Baltic are these. It is a little more to the south than the Baltic; it is about twice the area, and it connects with an interior which is not only vaster in extent, but infinitely richer in natural resources. The Baltic has played a great part in the history of Europe. As we were told, it was the scene, in the middle ages, of a great trade league that placed Europe on the map of the world, and in later years, we are sorry to say that it witnessed the rise of a nation that was so powerful as nearly to put Europe off the map. If the Hudson bay ever becomes to this continent one tithe of the value that the Baltic has been to Europe, it will certainly have a great history before it.
Its waters, its estuaries, its rivers, are simply teeming with all kinds of finny wealth, marketable, edible fish; and its interior, as we have been told to-night, abounds in mineral and animal wealth which some day will be of great commercial importance to this country. Now, as to the land that is traversed by the railway itself, I need hardly say that the resources of the district through which the Hudson Bay railway passes are forever beyond the sphere of speculation. In agricultural value, in mineral value, in fur, wood, pulp and power, that land can no longer be classified as barren. On the Nelson river alone it is estimated that there is a potentiality of 2,500,000 horse-power, which, as is well known, is equivalent to 20,000,000 tons of coal a year. And yet there are those who would contend that this country through which the Hudson Bay railway passes is a barren and impossible country. That 2,500,000 horse-power Is equal to our share in the possibilities of the St. Lawrence water scheme, and it is altogether our own, secure within the Canadian hinterland.

Now, our western wealth is not depen-' dent upon the products of our mines, and forests, and rivers. Our future depends on cur wheat fields, and some of us on this side of the House have been- yearning for the sight this spring which we have missed for the first time in many years. I refer to the young growing wheat, as with swift strokes it paints the prairies and the beautiful rolling lands to the north of the three provinces. To look upon a growing field of wheat through the yellow haze of a quiet spring night is one of those things which to have seen once is to love the West forever. Some of us have yearned for that sight during this spring. On an occasion of that kind you can almost hear nature making her promise of the great wealth ' of autumn. Our wheat crops, in quality and quantity and in ease of production, have no equal in this wide world. But unfortunately they have one almost fatal drawback, and that is their distance from the ultimate market. The Premier of Alberta, speaking recently, said that if our western crops were as near to the markets as the crops of Ontario they would be worth approximately 100 per cent more than at present. That is a very serious consideration for the western farmer, and added to that drawback there is the immense cost of production, which is another story. It is only under great difficulties that many of our western farmers, even in the best wheat growing districts, carry on at all; and if they were as sensitive in the matter of profits as other Canadian business men are they would have given up long ago. But the farmer is not so very sensitve to the rise and fall of profits. There is a good deal of elasticity about the economic position of the farmer. Rather than give in he will take it out of himself and unfortunately out of his family. He will take it out of his bank account rather than give in. I read the remarks of, I think, one of the British Columbia members, who I presume is a protectionist, who in going through a boot factory some time ago turned to one of the western farmers and said: "Would you put these people-mostly girls in their teens-out of work for the sake of a few cents on a pair of boots?" The obvious retort was: "Would you put hundreds of thousands of farmers out of business for the sake of a few cents a bushel on wheat?" And that is what it amounts to. The western farmer stays by it and he and his family sometimes suffer considerably. Here, then, we have a [ Mr. Bird. ]
scheme that brings the wheat belt within 500 or 600 miles of the sea; it brings us within easy touch of the seaboard, within a few miles as near to Liverpool as is Montreal. A speaker in this House said a short time ago that Montreal owes its superiority over Quebec as a seaport to the fact that it is 100 miles nearer to the sources of production than is Quebec. What would you say about a port 1,000 miles nearer the sources of production than Montreal? It could afford to have a good many more obstacles than it has at present. In order to put Montreal in the same position as Port Nelson with reference to the western wheat fields, you would have to transplant it to a point a little east of Winnipeg.
I think our contention goes a little deeper than I have already indicated. The western people are proud of the West. We do not talk so much about it perhaps as the eastern people do about the East, but we are just as proud of our country all the same. At the same time, while in the bottom of our hearts we are proud of it, we sometimes feel its isolation. I know I do, living 400 miles from any city of importance. We are hemmed in on all sides. To the west there is one of the world's greatest mountain ranges; to the south one of the world's greatest tariff walls; to the north the frozen regions inhospitable to man; and to the east a wilderness that is almost as forbidding as the frigid north. I wish I had more weight in order that what I say here might impress the House, but I want hon. members to feel that these conditions have had their influence upon the West in a way no easterner can imagine. No one who has not lived in the West can realize what these conditions have meant to those provinces during the last few years. They have welded us together, and given us a self-consciousness. They have brought us to the point where we have one outlook economically, one social feeling, one aspiration. One would think that in the West where we have such a miscellaneous population, of whom over 50 per cent are Europeans, there would be an ideal opportunity for the maximum of religious, racial and political friction, at least to a greater extent than in Ontario. But what do you find? In all these respects, in racial matters, in religious matters, in political matters, we have been brought together. We have been unified and at the present time we are at one in many

things. Those hon. gentlemen opposite or on the right who are looking for any serious reversion in the West to the old state of things, politically or in any other sense, are, I am afraid, inviting very serious disappointment to themselves, because they are leaving out of consideration the economic factors that have driven us together in recent years. Out West if Protestant and Catholic, Jew and Gentile, European and Canadian, and Grit and Tory did not get together and capitalize their humanity, life would not be worth living at all. They simply have to do it, and I should like this House to remember the tremendous urge that is behind the movement represented in this quarter of the Chamber.
So it would be unreasonable, Mr. Chairman to expect that such a large body of population as we have in the three prairie provinces existing under the same economic conditions practically one unit, a vigorous, ambitious, self-conscious people, should permanently be content to be frustrated of even a visionary hope of getting an avenue to the sea-the great way of commerce. I do not think it reasonable to expect that we will forever submit to being denied a "place in the sun".
Now, it would be very regrettable if any other section of Canada should obstinately refuse to the West this privilege because, mark you, Mr. Chairman, if you read history rightly, it is just the opposition to that kind of aspiration that causes all the trouble. We have heard a lot about the origin of the Great War. What was its origin? It was simply that the great bullying commercial nations of Europe denied to little Serbia its right to an avenue to the sea for the purposes of commerce. That was the beginning of the war. I do not think, in fact I am sure that there is no such sanguinary possibility in these circumstances, but statesmen are always willing to take into account the remotest considerations when the uniting of a great country like this is concerned.
I for one stand very solidly for the loyalty of the West, despite its 50 per cent European population. I think there is no section of Canada more loyal than the West. But, mark you, I am not inclined to get sentimental about it, just the same, because I recognize that loyalty, sterling virtue as it is, is always finally over-ridden by economic necessity-the first law of our being.
Now, as you pass up the St. Lawrence and enter Canada you are struck with one
feature in particular-those narrow strips of farms, so picturesque and peculiar, that run back from the water's edge away to the distant bush. I presume that that condition of things arose in the early days when the St. Lawrence was the only channel of inter-communication, and that the original settlers were indisposed to be pushed back into the interior and denied access to that channel. That method of planning out homesteads is not economically justifiable. But it has led to general contentment and has certain picturesque characteristics. But I mention that peculiarity because the feeling of the original settlers is something like that which the people of the West feel -they want to be at the front, to have a place at the water's edge. That is all the West wants. It wants a breathing point, an ocean avenue whereby it can come in touch with the rest of the world.
Coming into this building one notices this inscription above the doorway:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
I wonder who was responsible for selecting that inscription. It must have been some one who was against the Hudson Bay Railway proposition, I know. I think some day that couplet ought to be amended, and if I am a judge of poetry, you could not very well hurt its poetic qualities by adding these words:
-and the north.
I hope that amendment will be made so as to render the inscription apt and accurate to the condition of things which will then obtain.

Mr. Chairman, speaking in this House the other day I remarked that the people of western Canada believe that the case for the completion of the Hudson bay railway had been made out. That belief has been entertained for many years, and as long ago as I can remember in the West the people have referred to this project as feasible. In 1906,1 believe it was, the Hon. Walter Scott, the first Premier of Saskatchewan, speaking to a large audience of farmers of that province, remarked:
"The people of western Canada refuse to take their eyes off the Hudson bay route. For twenty years they have been looking that way."
That was in 1906. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) stated to-night that this project had been in the minds of the people of western Canada for forty years, and this is borne out by the facts. The Hon. Walter Scott continued:

UI have received an assurance that the Dominion government admit this project to be a national undertaking, and that they will not deny their responsibility."
It was a number of years later before the Dominion government assumed that responsibility.
I want, if possible, to make clear to this House some of the reasons why the people of western Canada believe that they have made out their case conclusively with regard to the Hudson bay project, and to this end I shall quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I believe the first time that in a public way the admission was made that this was a national undertaking, and would be undertaken in a national way, was at Niagara Palls in September 1908, and these are the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier as reported at that time:
"We have undertaken the construction of another railway, the Hudson bay railway. The Hudson's bay railway, I am sure, does not appeal very much to the people of Welland county. It concerns more the people of the West. But I say to you, gentlemen of Ontario, and you will agree with me, that what concerns one portion of the community concerns every part of the community. Now, we have come to the conclusion that this railway is a necessity, owing to the condition in which our fellow-citizens in the west are placed. This railway will give an alternative or optional route. At the present time all the wheat as soon as it is tracked is sent out to lake Superior. We want to provide another railway by Hudson's bay. There will then be the present route and the Hudson's bay route and the man who raises wheat and cattle will have two outlets for his production. We have been asked: "Are you not going to hurt the trade of the St. Lawrence, if you do that?'' Oh, ye of little faith! the trade of Canada is too great even for these two outlets. What we see coming will be more than sufficient for both the St. Lawrence and the Hudson's bay routes. We have come to the conclusion that the time to build this railway is now ; not to-morrow, but now; and we have surveyors in the field looking at the condition of the country and preparing plans for us, which we shall be prepared to put into execution as soon as we receive them. The Government will build the railway, or rather somebody will be entrusted with building it for us, but whatever we do, all the terminals and all the elevators shall be built by the Government, and retained under all and every circumstance by the Government so as to insure the [DOT] argest measure of benefit possible to the Canadian people in the North-West provinces.*'
Speaking that same year and referring to the speech of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. later Sir Robert Borden, said:
The Conservative party has been pledged to the building of that railway since 1S95, when it was promised by Sir Charles Tupper. The present Government has reached the same conclusion in the thirteenth year of its administration.

In the light of those statements, Mr. Chairman, I think it is only reasonable to assume that the people of western Canada believe their case is well made out, and they feel that if there is opposition to this route on the ground that it is not feasible, they have a right to claim that a report shall be made to them setting forth the circumstances in that respect.
I also want to place before the committee a few extracts from other reports which have been quoted in western Canada. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) has given to the committee tonight the last report that has been placed at our disposal, but for many years, at least since 1905, there have been a great number of reports made available to the people of this country on the Hudson bay project, and I believe that all these reports are now available to members of this House in the Library of this Parliament. I have gathered a few extracts from these reports which I shall give to the committee to show why the people of western Canada, having faith in the accuracy of these reports, believe they are justified in demanding that this route shall be carried through to completion.
The first extract is from a report made by Walter Dickson, for twenty years in the employ of the Hudson's Bay Company:
"From what I have observed of the movement of ice in Hudson bay during the summers I passed there I am perfectly assured that an ordinary screw steamer would never have any difficulty in getting through or around that ice which is usually met with in the bay or strait. The chief reason why the old sailing vessels of the Hudson's Bay Company often met with detention in the ice was that in the season when floe ice is met with, there is generally very little wind, and sailing vessels are as helpless amongst ice as they would be in a dead calm in the centre of the Atlantic or elsewhere. The bay has always been found of ready access to a good and careful navigator. From what is known, and my experience already obtained on the subject there is every reason to believe that were the Hudson bay thoroughly surveyed it would be found to be one of the safest of known seas. I have known the season when the harbours were accessible for seven months of the year.
Another captain in the employ of the Hudson's Bay Company, Janies Hackland, for thirty-nine years with the company, says:	"The strait is open all the year
round." Captain Colin Sinclair, for six years with the Hudson's Bay Company, says: "No unusual danger or difficulty in navigating the bay or strait." Captain Silsby, in the employ of the company from

Supply-Hudson Bay Ry.
1884, " saw no reason why steamships could not make excellent speed on that course to and from Europe for four months certainly in the year, and in open winters, five months." Captain Kennedy, with the company ror eight years, " found no ice after July first and only once on November first. The currents which open up the channel of ingress and egress are very regular and convert the bay and strait into a pathway for commerce."
These reports from which I have quoted, and similar reports, are probably the basis upon which the people of western Canada argue that the Hudson bay route is feasible. Their reason for requiring that route has been put before the committee with some detail in this debate by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, and I am not going .into that part of the question at this time. I simply want to point out that agriculturists in western Canada, in the position in which they find themselves at the present time are forced to look for every means which might alleviate their circumstances, and they have found that by attacking those things which were a hindrance to them and overcoming them, one by one, they have for a great many years been able to carry on in the face of countless obstacles. The cost of transportation before them at the present time is a problem they feel they must tackle and overcome. They believe that if this route were open, although it might not add greatly to the returns, would be of material help. The most optimistic figure is that if would add very materially to the returns, and that it might possibly mean all the difference between Fort William and Montreal, which is eleven or twelve cents a bushel, at the least. The most conservative estimate is that it would mean a difference of five cents a bushel on wheat, which at the present time would 'be something worth while for the western farmer.
Two or three hon. members who have spoken on this subject to-night have been so situated locally that this project appeals to them and their constituents in a personal way, because they are so close to the route and to the bay, comparatively speaking, but we must remember that all of western Canada is very much interested in this project, and not only western Canada but the northern states as well. It is perhaps not generally known that Winnipeg would be 600 miles closer to Liverpool via the Hudson bay route as compared with the railway route at the present time
via Montreal. Duluth would be 470 miles closer than it is via the Great lakes. St. Paul perhaps the greatest market in the western states for their grain, would be 150 miles closer to Liverpool via the Hudson bay route than it is via Chicago and Montreal. This is something that should be taken into account in considering this question.
In conclusion, I wish to refer to a letter I have in my hand, not that it has any particular bearing on the subject for, as I stated in the early part of my remarks, this is a national undertaking, as the Hon. Walter Scott said, and one which must be undertaken by the federal government, but it is from a correspondent who lives in a community which is in the unique position of having gone after a railroad and got it-not that they persuaded any great railway company to build for them, but when they could not get the railway company to build it they went to work and got out a charter and constructed the railway themselves. It is now a part of the Canadian National system. This correspondent urges me to take up this matter of the Hudson bay route, and suggests that if the Dominion of Canada is not in a position to finance it at the present time a charter should be granted to some of the western farmers, and they would finish the road themselves. He states in his letter that he is ready to pay $1,000 into any company that would be formed for that purpose, and he believes the project would meet with success. That shows you, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers of western Canada are not talking about this project as something which they believe in only theoretically, but they regard it as something that is absolutely practical.

After listening to the recent speeches, I cannot help but agree that the Hudson Bay railway is needed, and needed badly. I know something of the want of an outlet for the produce of our farms in the East, and while I do not live in western Canada, I believe that unless we can look at these questions from a broad national standpoint and be willing to help the other fellow as well as ourselves, we shall not get very far. Compare this now with the methods devised by the present administration in the expenditure of public moneys on those vast transportation systems. Both in the case of the Canadian National railway and the merchant marine, the government has constituted boards of management. These boards are composed almost exclusively of the government's own friends; almost without exception the gentlemen who compose these boards are associated with large industrial enterprises and businesses which are engaged in the manufacture, selling

Coming back again to the question of the Hudson Bay railway, I can remember away back about 1891, not long after I came to Canada, one of the leading papers in the West had a cartoon in which appeared a locomotive, with the engine driver sitting at the lever, just about ready to start. A questioner came up, and said, "Well, sir, what do you hope to carry over this road anyway?"' And the driver replied, "The province, my dear sir, the province." The engineer happened to be Sir Charles Tupper- This road for the last forty years has been made the political football of the parties, and I think it is about time that we dealt with these matters with some broad outlook for the future. I do not wonder that this has been the case, particularly after the information that my hon. friend in front of m/e has given to the House to-night. This Hudson Bay railway is one of the necessities of the present time, and has been for many years. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in the West in 1911 he said this line would be built as soon as the survey could be made and the feasibility established, with ports, terminals and everything under governmental control and ownership. Later on, it was promised by Sir Robert Borden, and after the change took place in 1911, when the call from the West became so insistent that it could not be put down, the construction of the road was begun. Some $21,000,000, I believe, has been spent on this road already, and it will take somewhere about $2,000,000 more to complete it. For many miles north of the Pas at the present time the steel is laid, and the grade has already been made to tide water. The steel has been left to rust and the grade has been left to crumble down, and it is time we looked after this to prevent the deterioration of the work that has been done. I know that, during all this time, this railway has been viewed with hostility by interests in the East, by those cities and railways which are benefiting by keeping the commerce of the western prairies coming this way to its ultimate market. The plea has been put forward that we have no money, notwithstanding the fact that millions of dollars have been voted for other purposes, which, to say the least, are of questionable benefit to the country at this time. But now that the war is over and labour is plentiful, we find the counter proposal put forward, which is attracting interest in the East at the present time, namely, the deep waterway scheme to the head of the lakes. We are told that nearly half a billion dollars can be found for this scheme, while $2,000,000 cannot be found for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
Indeed, I think it would not be out of place to make some few comparisons between these two schemes at the present time. The deep waterway project can be used possibly for seven months of the year, and we might compare the cost of the completion of this scheme with the paltry sum that is needed to complete a route to what will, perhaps, be and is admitted to be one of the finest harbours on the North American continent, if a deep sea harbour at the least possible cost can be constructed. Some doubt may be expressed as to the feasibility of this route; but this great inland sea seems to have been placed there by Providence for an outlet for what is, perhaps, the largest pastoral and grain growing area in the world. It is a route to the great West, and part of the immense domain that was seized on by that great trading company, the Hudson's Bay Company, over two centuries ago to take in supplies and carry out the produce gathered from the natives in barter. We know that, during

Hudson Bay Ry.

all that time, this great company did not lose one ship by ice or storm, and its captains of navigation have told us that they have gone in and out through those straits at any time of the year that they have been ready. We have been told that this great inland sea is one frozen mass of ice during the winter. This is not so. With the great volume of fresh water flowing into the bay every day through such streams as the Nelson river, the Churchill river, the Severn river and, perhaps, half a dozen other streams just as important, meeting the tide there which comes up through those straits every twenty-four hours, and all having to go out again, it is impossible that any ice could be formed except some shale ice on the shores. We used to be told that the country round about was one desert on which nothing could grow, on which human beings could not live. We know that now to be a fallacy, and that the railway would pay for itself independently of the traffic and commerce that might go out through the Hudson Bay strait. Anyone at all familiar with salt water will know that it is many degrees warmer than fresh water, and as compared with lake Superior, this is a fact. When we know that there is a rise and fall of a good many feet every twenty-four hours, we must realize that it is impossible that ice should form. We have been given a good deal of information about this route by certain expeditions, some of which before now have wintered in Hudson bay. Perhaps one of the most complete reports is that given by Captain Preakly before the committee here in 1920. Some extracts from his evidence are certainly very interesting. I do not think I need weary the House with much reading; but he says:
There are no icebergs in Fox channel or Hudson bay and comparatively few in the west end of Hudson straits, but numerous in the eastern portion of the straits.
He informs us of some of the peculiarities of the bay, where a strong current goes west from the straits and practically goes all around that great inland sea, attaining sometimes a velocity of seven miles an hour and keeping all ice moving at any time of the year.
I am convinced that the Hudson Bay Railway is the only salvation for agriculture on the western prairies. For instance, a trainload of cattle could be landed at the bay terminus of the Hudson Bay Railway in just about one-third of the time that it takes now to land them at any point where they can be transferred to

ocean-going steamers. This would mean a saving in feed and care of nearly four days, besides the tremendous shrinkage in weight consequent upon the movement of livestock. The advantage in mileage of this route is not generally realized, say from the centre of the wheat belt to the bay. Moreover, the producing area of the West, either in grain raising or for pastoral pursuits runs up very close to the bay itself, and I believe the northern limitation of wheat can be very much extended yet as the right varieties are propagated. From Saskatoon, which is about the heart of the wheat growing belt, it is 742 miles to tide water on the present route of the Hudson Bay Railway. From Saskatoon to Fort William it is 900 miles, and then we are further away from Liverpool than we are at Hudson bay. On this account alone, there would be a saving of over 160 miles, or over one and one-half day's travel. But even after getting to Fort William there is still 1,000 miles of a haul before the grain can reach the seaboard. The distance from Saskatoon to Liverpool via St. John in the winter months is 4,996 miles; from Saskatoon via Montreal in the summer months it is 4,587 miles; from Port Nelson to Liverpool the distance is only 3,708 miles, or a distinct saving of 879 miles over the route via Montreal and a distinct saving of 1,280 miles over the route via St. John. The utility of this route is unquestionable, if we only consider that it is important to the people of the West to be within one day's run to the ocean where the fish may come down to the millions who occupy the prairies, as well as the millions yet to come.
Again, we must not lose sight of the fact that the St. Lawrence carries about the highest rate of insurance of any navigable route in the world, while here is a route that has been used for 40 years now by people we know and who can speak of it with some knowledge. Sailing vessels have gone in and out any time of the year they were ready. When we consider the cost it means the difference between success and failure to the prairie provinces to-day. There will be a saving of at least 5 cents a bushel between Hudson bay and the present route to the present terminal at Fort William. The time has come when it is absolutely necessary to lower the cost of production on the prairies if agriculture is to continue there. Even if we did have the deep waterway to the head of the lakes we have a road that could be open six and a half or seven months at the outside

during the year. But I am convinced from what I have read from the evidence contained in this bulletin that navigation can be carried on for at least five months in the year with safety, as compared with any other navigable route in any part of the world. Several of the most valuable minerals are found along the route of the railway, besides timber, game, fish, etc. I think, therefore, that the work should be done. All the boards of trade as well as the farmers' organisations of western Canada are anxiously looking to the Government to complete this work, believing that it is going to be of great service to that part of the Dominion. Besides, the work already done is deteriorating, and much labour and material is going to waste. It is not too late yet to provide for this matter in the estimates for the present year. There is no scarcity of labour, and in fact thousands of men are anxiously waiting to get work. I do not think there was ever a more opportune time than the present to carry this work to a completion, and I should like to know what the policy of the Government is regarding the scheme. Are we to take it now that the policy of the Government is represented in this estimate of $40,000 for the care of terminals this year? The Government should let us know whether they intend to complete this road at the earliest possible moment, and what reason there is why the work cannot be proceeded with at the present time.

I think it is time we had a change in this programme. Most of the Progressive members speak of the West as though it comprised just Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. One would imagine that these were the only places in the West. Well, I consider that coming from British Columbia I come from the West. We have heard a great deal of the Hudson Bay railway, and I do not object to hon. members putting their claims before the Government. I think that is their legitimate right and they should get every consideration. But I want to point out that we have been promised a railway in British Columbia for many years now. It was left in abeyance until the close of the war, and when the war was over the late government started work on it to give employment to returned men. Now I am told that between 200 and 300 of these men have bought land along that road and have settled, expecting the road to be completed and that they would then have transportation. I am referring to the railway between Kamloops and Kelowna. According
to a report I have received from the Minister of Railways, there has been $5,265,000 spent on this railway, and it requires a little over $1,250,000 to complete it. The ties are there, the bridges are in, the rails are very largely there, and everything is ready to complete the work. This road would be one of the greatest feeders that the Canadian National system could have. It would take practically all of the freight from the Okanagan valley to the Canadian National railway which is now taken by the Canadian Pacific railway. I do not complain because the Canadian Pacific railway has this freight, but I think that we should look to the interests of our own railways, and the Minister of Railways ought to see that this line is completed at the earliest possible date.

I just want to add a
word to the discussion on the Hudson bay question, It is not considered very seriously by some people, but this is perhaps because of their lack of appreciation of the facts. Now, I would not ask to-night, nor in the near future, for what the people are hoping for in the district in which I live. We have great possibilities in our mines, and we ourselves can hardly conceive the undeveloped natural resources that we have. We would not ask that the Hudson Bay railway be completed for our especial benefit at the present time, but there is a hope that some time when that road is completed there will be built a connecting line between our district and Fort Church-hill, which is not more than about 800 miles from Edmonton. But the Hudson Bay railway must be completed before we ask for anything of that kind. Naturally, of course, we are looking forward to the time when that can be done. The people in the wheat fields of Saskatchewan are more directly interested in the matter than perhaps we are, but I have been practically half way across from Edmonton to Fort Churchill, and have seen people already settled in that country from 125 to 150 miles distant from railways, who are anxiously waiting for railway accommodation. A large portion of that country is suitable for settlement. There is other wealth there besides agriculture, and I found that in places thousands of tons of hay could be cut if there were transportation facilities; but in the present state of things it is simply going to waste. Perhaps such a railroad at this time would not pay, but we are looking ahead to when it would be not only advisable but neces-

sary, for I have no doubt that the Hudson bay route is feasible. There is no question about the desirability of the Hudson bay route, but we will never know whether it will be a practicable outlet until we try it, and the people in our part of the country are very anxious that this should be settled one way or the other.
I feel that Canadians generally do not realize the immense potentialities of that part of the Dominion, and I believe that it is our own lack of enterprise rather than any natural handicap which has held back its development. I know people who are developing that country successfully, but they are very much discouraged by reason of lack of transportation facilities, and they will not continue their work until such facilities are provided. For instance, fish teem in the lakes there, and I heard a man state before the Board of Trade of Edmonton last winter-he was interested in a fishing company-that it cost as much to send fish from a small town on the Great Waterways railway to Edmonton as from the Pacific Coast clear through to Winnipeg. Therefore if a road were constructed from that country eastwards it would afford an outlet for the great mineral, agricultural and: timber and fisheries wealth of that extensive country.
The people of Alberta join with the people of Saskatchewan in the hope that some tilne a railroad will he built through to Fort Churchill and so afford an outlet for the cattle, grain and other products of the settlers who are developing that country.
What is the ipolicy of the Government regarding this road?

I am sure that every member, irrespective of the constituency he represents or his party affiliations, is interested in the transportation facilities of the West. It does not matter very much to most of us whether the grain be shipped eastward via the Great Lakes, westward to the Pacific coast, or northward, to Hudson hay; but we are all interested in seeing that every facility shall be afforded the grain growers of the West to market their grain at the lowest possible cost.
This Hudson bay project, as has been stated to-night, has cost so far approximately $20,000,000. The estimates I have seen indicate that it will take another $5,000,000 to complete the railway to the

bay, and an additional $10,000,000 to complete the terminal facilities.
We have been told to-night that notwithstanding our expenditure of $6,000,000 at Fort Nelson we should abandon that port and select Fort Churchill as the terminal. You can readily see, Mr. Chairman, that the Government can scarcely be expected to give an immediate answer to the question submitted to it when even among those who are advocating the completion of the project there is no unanimity of opinion. I did tell the delegation which the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) referred to this afternoon that when the new board of directors of the Canadian National Railways was organized the matter would be brought to their attention, and I have no doubt they will at the earliest possible date give it the consideration it deserves.
Is there a likehood of an investigation this season of the desirability of selecting Fort Churchill as the terminal?

I am not
in a position to answer the question at the present time. That matter will have to be determined by the incoming board.

Was not an exhaustive
investigation made some time ago?

Yes, some
years ago.

There will be no tendency
on the part of the Government to allow this matter to drop?

There is
not any tendency on the part of the Government to refrain from doing anything which they conceive to be in the public interest, and when the opportunity offers- as we hope it will at an early date- this problem, among many others, will be taken into consideration.

Just a word of explanation as to this item. The committee will observe that as compared with the estimates of last year there is a decrease of $700,470.85. I might explain for the information of the committee that this decrease is due in the first place to the dropping of a number of positions whose incumbents have left the service; secondly, to the reduction of the amount required for temporary assistance during the year; and thirdly, to the dropping of an amount that was formerly voted for what is called a provisional allowance, but which has been replaced by the cost of living bonus.

An hon. member desired me to get certain information as he could not be here. It is as to the greater use of our National Railway system for the carrying of the mails. I am not prepared, as he was, to discuss it fully, but I should like to bring to my hon. friend's attention the situation which exists to-day in British Columbia, and I have no doubt it is duplicated in other sections of the country, not through any intentional neglect on the part of the department, I believe, but through the growth and development of the National Railways in recent years.
There is a section between the city of Kamloops and the northern part of British Columbia served by the Canadian National Railways. Any mail that is posted in that district is carried to the city of Kamloops, then down by the Canadian Pacific to Vancouver; it goes into the post office at Kamloops and is sorted there, I believe, causing a delay, whereas the Canadian National runs daily trains right into Vancouver, and the mails could be carried on just the same schedule as the Canadian Pacific makes, the Canadian Pacific not touching the district at all.
There was the question also of sending mail into the considerable town of Prince George. The Canadian National could very well carry that mail from Vancouver to the Yellowhead, and then send it back on the Grand Trunk Pacific into Prince George. At the present time we send it all up the coast five hundred miles by Prince Rupert, a much longer distance, to Prince George and taking perhaps a day longer, and costing as much if not more. What I wish to say is this. I think a careful study should be made of the whole mail service, and that more business should be given to our National Railways than they are receiving at the present time. This is somewhat a large question to enter into in any extensive manner, and I am merely giving a very rough outline and simply enunciating what I think is the principle that should be adopted.
I may add this. We now have a schedule on the Canadian National Railways from Montreal to the Pacific coast that equals the Canadian Pacific schedule. They do not carry mail, I understand, on their fast trans-Canada train, but No. 1 on the Canadian Pacific and No. 1 on the Canadian National have a similar schedule; one is just as fast as the other, and there is no reason in the world why a great deal more of the mail of this country should not be carried over the National railways.

The matter to which my hon. friend has drawn the attention of the committee, as well as of the department, is one of very great importance to the great province which he has the honour to represent in this House. I may inform him and the committee that the whole question is a very wide one and entails a good deal of consideration, much investigation, and a careful decision after these preliminaries have been carried out. It happens that at the present time such an inquiry is under way, and after the House prorogues it is the intention of the department to have one of the inspectors go over the whole route between here and the coast with a view to determining on the spot what changes can be made in the direction indicated by my hon. friend. Wherever it is possible to do so, preference will be given to the carriage of the mails by the National Railways, but this has to be borne in mind, that in view of the economy prescribed by the Minister of Finance, and of the financial condition of the country, with which my hon. friend is as fully conversant as I am, regard must be had to the cost of carrying the mail. Just on that point I might explain that in connection with one of the new railway services, the establishment of a daily train service between Edmonton and Prince Rupert, application was made for a corresponding change in the mail service; that is, instead of a tri-weekly , mail service, there should be established a daily mail service. At first glance that seemed the most natural thing in the world and personally, before seeking the advice of the officials of the department, I was inclined to favour it, but a few days later, after the matter had been thoroughly gone into, and I found from the reports presented to me that even this seemingly proper change and, at a superficial glance, this small change would alone entail an extra expenditure of nearly $75,000. Well, I had to hesitate before giving any instructions for the adoption of this change. I mention this merely as one illustration of how much money even an apparently slight change will run into. However, I can assure my hon. friend and the committee that special attention is being given to the postal service generally, and British Columbia will receive its full share of attention in this regard.

with respect to the establishment of new rural free delivery routes.
